subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT SUPPLEMENTARY IMPORTS OF POULTRY FROM U.S. BE STOPPED-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I seek the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, considering the dire straits in which the chicken industry is in Quebec and in all Canada.
Yesterday I received a copy of a telegram which the Quebec poultry producers' union sent to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) in which they urged him to order an immediate stop to any issue of supplementary import quotas to the United States, since the present inventories and physical production facilities are sufficient to meet the demand of the Canadian market. Besides, the Quebec Federation des producteurs de volailles, supported by the UPA, is worried about the excess production of chicken piling up in storage facilities in Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia. Therefore, 1 move:
That the government give instructions to have any supplementary imports of chicken from the United States stopped immediately, that the agreement on import quotas with the United States be re-negotiated to the level of egg import quotas, that the government submit the request of Canadian producers to GATT arbitration if the Americans disagree.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN PENSIONS OF PERSONS INJURED IN 1917 HALIFAX EXPLOSION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
I rise, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Sixty-two years ago today, in history's largest nonnuclear explosion, 2,000 citizens of Halifax were killed and
9,000	injured following a collision in Halifax harbour of a munitions ship bound for the front lines during World War I. Fifty-two people still receive spouse's pensions, or pensions for blindness caused by the explosion, fixed at only 71 per cent of the equivalent pensions received by combat veterans of World War I.
In view of the inadequacy of these pensions, in many cases, to meet the requirements of the recipients, and in view of the understanding long held by many that pensions would be paid as if the explosion had occurred at the front lines, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby), and concurred in by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That, in the opinion of this House, the government consider bringing forward legislation at the earliest opportunity to increase pensions to those injured in the Halifax explosion to the same levels as those received by other World War I casualties.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REINSTATEMENT OF IMMIGRATION POLICY FOR BOAT PEOPLE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. Yesterday the minister announced yet another flip-flop in government policy, namely, that he would be reversing the very successful boat people matching program. The new leadership which the government is providing means that for every boat person sponsored by private citizens, our government will sponsor one less, rather than one more. 1 believe the minister and the government are caving in to the backlash. Will the hon. gentleman not acknowledge that the people have been misled by this reversal of policy? Will he not change his mind and reinstate one of the most successful programs he has established, and abandon this reactionary change?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ron Atkey (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REINSTATEMENT OF IMMIGRATION POLICY FOR BOAT PEOPLE
speechtext:
The commitment of this government to accept 50,000 refugees by the end of 1980 remains firm. That is the Canadian commitment which will consist of privately sponsored refugees and government sponsored refugees. Twenty-one thousand of those refugees have already arrived on our shores; the balance will be coming, hopefully, within less than a year.
Rather than a "caving in", as the hon. member alleges, this is an expansion of the program because we have suddenly recognized-it was not really sudden, though it may have been sudden for the hon. member opposite-the very serious problem which exists in Kampuchea and in Thailand, where some
600,000	people are fleeing for their very lives. We want to free up sufficient funds from the existing program through a shift from government to private sponsorship. This will enable Canadian contributions of food and medical aid to be given to the unfortunate victims in Kampuchea. That is an expansion of the government's program.

December 6, 1979
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REINSTATEMENT OF IMMIGRATION POLICY FOR BOAT PEOPLE
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister further about this so-called expansion. In the statement this morning, the hon. gentleman announced that $1,300 would be saved by each of the non-sponsored refugees.

subtopic: PLANS TO DEAL WITH POSSIBLE OIL SHORTAGE THIS WINTER
PLANS TO DEAL WITH POSSIBLE OIL SHORTAGE THIS WINTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Does the minister agree with the statement made by the Prime Minister yesterday in this House concerning oil supplies that, and I quote:
The National Energy Board has now, as a result of increased consumption in Canada and some other activities, come to the conclusion that there may be limited shortages this winter in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: PLANS TO DEAL WITH POSSIBLE OIL SHORTAGE THIS WINTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always agree with the Prime Minister, who is always very perceptive with respect to this particular situation. The fact of the matter is that 1 indicated to the hon. member in committee this morning-and I mentioned this during the course of preceding months this fall and last summer-that we are and have been in a very tight situation in Canada. Naturally, in a tight situation there are going to be circumstances in which there could, indeed, be shortages of a temporary nature.
We are hoping that the situation will not deteriorate any further. We are continuing to take steps, on a daily basis, in consultation with importers and industry in general, to try to tide us through this winter. The Prime Minister is right: there could very well be interruptions in terms of supply in the course of this winter. But we are doing everything possible to avoid that situation and we are taking every initiative we can.

subtopic: PLANS TO DEAL WITH POSSIBLE OIL SHORTAGE THIS WINTER
speechtext:
Now that we have that clear admission about the possibility of shortages, the question is what action the government is prepared to take. In that regard, 1 have a question for the minister which relates to a confidential report given to him last week by the National Energy Board, since revealed somewhat in the text of the telegram 1 have here from the board to the deputy minister of energy in Ontario, sent two days ago, in which the minister was advised of the very precarious situation in eastern Canada and that we would need an additional 2 million barrels of distillates as of the end of November.
Oral Questions
Given the fact that now diesel and home heating oil supplies are down 15 per cent in Ontario and eastern Canada over the same amount last year at this time, what specific action is the government taking to make up this shortfall so that the shortages will not, in fact, happen over the next few months?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: PLANS TO DEAL WITH POSSIBLE OIL SHORTAGE THIS WINTER
speechtext:
1 have indicated on previous occasions, as well, that we are in a position, after the actions taken under the previous administration, of building up the inventories in our country to an acceptable level. It is quite true that we have been striving to accomplish that over the time we have had this responsibility as the government. The fact is that I and my department, in the course of discussions with industry, have been working very closely with them to determine what can be done in the way of import requirements on the part of each of the companies, and what we can do to bring in additional product in order to meet our requirements this winter.
There have been instances, which 1 have mentioned in the House, of various companies, such as Imperial and Gulf, being able to indicate that they will be obtaining additional imports of product for us to help tide us through the winter.

subtopic: PLANS TO DEAL WITH POSSIBLE OIL SHORTAGE THIS WINTER
speechtext:
The National Energy Board indicated to the minister that there were three courses of action that could be taken to try to alleviate the supply problem. The minister has alluded to one, which is increasing imports. The other was instructing refineries to convert from gasoline production to home heating production. The third was curtailing exports. It is in the latter regard that I should like to put a question to the minister.
Given the fact that we are currently exporting 75,000 barrels a day of fuel oil products, half of which are home heating oil supplies, and given this precarious supply situation, is the minister prepared, today, to recommend to the National Energy Board the cancellation or curtailment of those exports to the United States? Surely Canadian interests come first in this case.

subtopic: PLANS TO DEAL WITH POSSIBLE OIL SHORTAGE THIS WINTER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: PLANS TO DEAL WITH POSSIBLE OIL SHORTAGE THIS WINTER
speechtext:
In fact, as the hon. member knows, the National Energy Board has Canadian interests very much in mind as part of its mandate with respect to applications for exports of product, and this is a prerequisite and a condition upon which any licence for export is undertaken. The fact of the matter is that we are canvassing a number of possibilities to increase the inventory we have. 1 have taken steps to reduce general exports in terms of crude to the United States, to supply our domestic needs.
Naturally, I will be glad to look into the matter raised by the hon. member with the National Energy Board and receive an up-to-date report from them, so that I can assure the hon. member that I am taking all steps to get us through the winter, all steps available to us in light of the situation in which we find ourselves.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is also directed to the hon. Minister of Agriculture.
Given the telegram forwarded by the Union des producteurs agricoles to the right hon. Prime Minister, can the minister tell us what consultations he had with the Quebec government and with UPA representatives? subtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING NEGOTIATIONS WITH QUEBEC AND POULTRY PRODUCERS' UNION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I have indicated on a number of occasions, I communicate very regularly and quite frequently with my Quebec counterpart. If there is any question on any member's mind in the House as to the inability of the minister of agriculture of the province of Quebec to communicate his feelings to the Minister of Agriculture of Canada, they should remove those doubts immediately. To come to the last question, the National Energy Board has now, as a result of increased consumption in Canada and some other activities, come to the conclusion that there may be limited shortages this winter in Canada.

Prime Minister, is now forced to amend the content of its report. I do not want to hold up the work of the House unduly, Mr. Speaker. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, during the question period when the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) was answering my questions with respect to the appointment of ministers to answer questions in this House, the Prime Minister refused to acknowledge that in our system of responsible government, senior ministers-

speechtext:

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. ALLMAND-MINISTERS NOT MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace will know that he will have to identify the nature of his question of privilege to me. If it is simply a grievance that ministers of the Crown sit outside of the House of Commons, he will know that that is a repetition of previous practices of the House, and while it may be an annoyance and a matter of commentary, it does not constitute a procedural problem in which the Chair can be expected to intervene. If he has some special nature of the matter which does bring it within the orbit of privilege, I will be glad to hear it.

subtopic: MR. ALLMAND-MINISTERS NOT MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the special aspect that I would argue strongly for is that the Minister of Justice, who is the
Point of Order-Mr. Lalonde
Attorney General of Canada, has very special responsibilities in the laying of legal actions and so on which cannot be answered for by any other minister, because he is sworn in as Attorney General and Minister of Justice. I would argue that only he and not the ministers who are designated can answer these questions. In our parliamentary system of responsible government, it is not correct for such a procedure to continue. 1 can understand an Acting Minister of Justice sitting in the Senate on a temporary basis, but this situation is completely against our system of responsible government. There has been an opportunity in Prince Albert and in Newfoundland for that minister to run in an election and be elected.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. ALLMAND-MINISTERS NOT MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Order, please. Again, I would remind the hon. member that he is raising a matter which he considers to be a grievance. That may be so, and it may be an annoyance upon which he may make a comment, as he has done. 1 cannot bring the matter within the realm of procedure. It is the right of the government, and it is in keeping with previous parliamentary practice, whether it be the Minister of Justice or, as in a previous case, the Minister of National Revenue, to have ministers who sit outside the House for a period of time. There is no necessity, in fact, that all the ministers even be members of the House of Commons or the Senate. Therefore, I am not able to act on procedural grounds on the hon. member's case.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: That this House deplores the complete inaction of the government, after six months in office, with regard to the creation of jobs, regrets the inhumane cutbacks in the Canada Works program that have eliminated hundreds of communities across Canada that have been suffering from high levels of unemployment and condemns the government for its failure to date to bring forward a comprehensive employment strategy for the coming year.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: Hon. members will note that not later than 9.45 p.m. this evening, pursuant to Standing Order 32(1 )(k), proceedings on this motion shall expire in accordance with that order and also with Standing Order 58(10).

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago during question period in the House, we celebrated-of course "celebrated" may not be the right word because this is certainly not cause for celebration throughout the country-let us say therefore that we noted the first six months in power of our colleagues on the other side of the House. Mr. Speaker, we would have liked on that occasion to be able to tell members opposite, and more especially the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Atkey), that they had done a good job.
Unfortunately, the only thing we have seen in the last six months has been nearly complete inaction. This is why, Mr. Speaker, after six months of this government, after six months of having the hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration on the job, we would like to tell him that he has yet to present to the House and to the Canadian people an employment strategy for the forthcoming months.
Mr. Speaker, it is not normal to wait until just before Christmas, until mid-December, until snow is coming down throughout the country, to present an employment strategy for the current year. This year is coming to an end and we are entitled to ask the minister to tell us about his plans not only for the forthcoming months, but more important, for next summer and next fall.
The minister has thrown away six months of lead time that was given to him by the previous government. He inherited a position where job creation was strong, where we led most of our trading partners in the area of job creation. The minister benefited from a situation where the rate of unemployment dropped for 14 consecutive months in this country. He inherited a situation where the economy was still strong, in spite of the fact that there were turnarounds on the horizon, turn-

December 6, 1979
Employment Strategy
arounds caused in many instances by events occurring outside our borders. The economic climate has deteriorated a great deal, and in spite of that his response has continued to be to do nothing. Since taking office the first response of the minister, whose responsibility it is to try to create employment in this country, in his first interviews on television, was to say that he thought his position within the cabinet was one of creating "jobs, jobs, jobs". These were the words he used. Since that time we have seen no concrete measures or steps but we have heard speeches and a lot of rhetoric, in spite of the fact that the economic climate has indeed changed and requires new steps to be taken to stimulate the economy and create employment in this country.
The minister knows full well that there is a recession in the United States. Surely he knows, as do his advisers, that the recession in the United States will have deeply-felt repercussions on the Canadian economy. When our major trading partner goes into a state of slow growth, it is evident that we will be trading less with them and that there will be grave repercussions in the factories, in industry and in commerce in general throughout this country with the consequent loss of jobs.
That is not the only thing, Mr. Speaker. There have also been successive increases in interest rates. The bank rate, as we all know, has now climbed to 14 per cent. Prime rates charged by the chartered banks to their best industrial customers have now climbed to 15 per cent, putting businessmen in a precarious position. Plant closures, which have been brought to the minister's attention time and time again, have begun to occur, with many of the people involved pointing directly to the high interest rates subscribed to by this government as the main cause of those closings. We also hear about unfortunate problems encountered by the employees of Chrysler in the Windsor area and the employees of ITT in northern Quebec. We hear of the problems in shipyards, and there is a general situation of slow growth in the country. But the minister, whose main responsibility it is to bring about job creation and employment opportunities in this country, does nothing.
What about the most important policy direction of this government? The most important policy direction of this government is to raise oil prices to 90 per cent of the Chicago price. We all know that while the domestic price of oil in Toronto today is around SI5.63 a barrel, the Chicago price j>y 1985 will be around $43.46, according to figures published by the minister's colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn), and it will be reaching about $62.81 by 1990, which will be slightly higher than the international price.
One of the stated objectives of this government is to raise the domestic price of oil slightly above the international price, thus taking away one of the main advantages that industry, trade and commerce has in this country in dealing with competitors outside of our borders. Where does the Minister of Employment and Immigration stand on this question? We have not heard him say anything about this matter. We have not heard him take a stand against the scandalous increases in

the price of oil, despite the fact that the minister knows full well that these increases will have dire consequences on our economy.
1 am not quite sure whether the minister has actually examined the effect which such policies will have on employment in this country. Perhaps 1 could quote to him the already well-known study that has been done on the economic impact of oil prices, because the minister tells me his department does not do any studies on the economic impact on the country of changes in the interest rate or increases in the oil price; he leaves that to the Department of Finance, although 1 would expect him to act on that and bring forward new policies when such drastic changes in the economic picture of the country are taking place.
Let us look at what the Conservative Premier of Ontario is telling the Minister of Employment and Immigration through his colleague, the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark). He is telling him that these increases in the price of oil will have a drastic effect on the Canadian economy, particularly on the job-creation sector in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: What do the other nine say?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext:
Let us stick for the moment with the Premier of Ontario. If the hon. member thinks that increases in oil prices will increase job creation in Canada, 1 should like him to quote the name of the economist who said that. So far as the Conservative government of Ontario is concerned, their main conclusion is that by the end of 1981 consumer prices will be 4.5 per cent higher. In the area of job creation there will be 137,000 fewer jobs, which is probably a greater destruction of jobs during the course of the possible tenure of the minister than the total number of jobs he will create in that period of time. The way things are going now, the minister should be concerned he will end up with fewer jobs by 1981 than we would have had without this. By the end of 1981 we are talking about 137,000 fewer jobs in this country. We are talking about a real gross national product of 2 per cent less, if these oil price increases are indeed brought forward by this government, than would be the case.
Let me digress for one moment to say that not only is the government talking about slowing down the economy and doing it in a purposeful fashion by increasing the price of oil, but they are also talking about taking 30 cents a gallon out of the pocket of every car owner in this country. When the Prime Minister speaks about qn excise tax of 30 cents a gallon, he is also telling us he will; take around $2.8 billion out of the pockets; of car owners 'across the country, and that too will have a significant impact on job creation.
As I (have said, we hqve heard speeches today. From the beginning of his mandat^ this summer, the minister has promised us a number of iniiiatives in the job-creation field. He spoke about youth employment. He told us he will be seeing some of these initiatives taking place in the early fall. It is almost early winter and we have yet to see them. To date the only thing he has actually done has been to go the other way. Not only has he not created jobs; he has decided, in a cold
December 6, 1979

blooded fashion, to decrease the amount of money available in this country for job-creation purposes. His response to date has been to cut back on the Canada Works program and make cutbacks in the LEDA program.
The minister will tell me that what he is interested in doing is creating permanent jobs, and I agree with him. I too am interested in creating permanent jobs. But what the minister is saying is that he can do away with some of this temporary job creation, and what I am telling the minister is that in a country like Canada where there is a cyclical slowdown in the economy, what he is doing really is telling people that they will be on unemployment insurance or welfare during the winter months instead of being able to benefit from programs such as Canada Works. Instead of being able to fulfil strong local community objectives and needs, they will be collecting unemployment insurance cheques, in spite of the fact that these people would much rather work.
1 do not want to insist only on increased use of the Canada Works program because I am reminded that our own employment strategy a year ago included a number of initiatives which, from reading the minister's speeches, I see he will try to wrap up and put a ribbon on, perhaps because it is Christmas and time to deliver a new package to the Canadian public. When I look at the employment strategy which was brought down in September of 1978 by the Hon. Bud Cullen, I see that already at that time there was under way an employment tax credit program of $106 million. 1 see also that there was a summer youth employment program of $116 million, there were year-round youth employment measures of $109.7 million, there was a JET program in existence at the time, there was the Canada Works program and a skilled training program of $101.5 million. In this sense 1 hope the minister will be continuing the initiatives of his predecessor in the skilled training area because I really think this is one of the most important areas with which we have to be involved in the years to come.
I have with me a copy of the sixteenth annual review of the Economic Council of Canada. One of their recommendations touches upon labour market policies. It hits home in one of the most important areas of job creation in Canada, and that is shortages of skilled manpower. It is one thing to create jobs in the immediate future, and it is one thing to try and create temporary jobs to get over periods of high unemployment. But it is another thing to deal with skilled shortages, something to which the previous government allocated substantial funds. I hope the minister will continue with that thrust.
I should like to quote from the sixteenth annual review of the Economic Council of Canada entitled: "Two Cheers for the Eighties" at page 87, which reads as follows:
It is apparent that as we enter the 1980s, skilled shortages ... will get worse. This has major implications for occupational forecasting and training programs. Clearly, appropriate treatment of labour market imbalances depends crucially on accurate and timely diagnosis. A critical review is needed of the capabilities of Canadian government and industry in forecasting the demand and supply of
Employment Strategy
occupational skills, translating these into skill-training requirements, and mounting effective training programs.
One of the major recommendations of the council was that the federal government, in conjunction with the provinces, should reassess the present programs with a view to tailoring them more efficiently for labour market needs of the 1980s.
The minister made a speech in front of the Canadian Club in Toronto. He talked about critical skill training programs. 1 applaud that type of remark because I think in that regard he is indeed on the right track. But instead of cutting back his job-creation programs, if he is going to transfer funds to other areas of his department I trust that he will cease the practice he has been involved in since the beginning of the year of transferring funds to purposes other than job-creation purposes, and that he will think in terms of transferring them to this type of program.
This brings me to the Canada Works program which is mentioned quite specifically in the motion. In that regard not only is the minister not content to decrease the amount of money put into the Canada Works program this year by something over $40 million, but also he talks of eliminating the program completely next year. Perhaps moneys can be used in a better way, but the minister has yet to tell us what that better way is. It is really incumbent upon him, before eliminating programs in such a complete and drastic fashion, to tell us what he is going to do with the program and where he is going to spend the money. It would be a good idea if now and then he told Parliament what he was going to do or what he has in mind, instead of telling the Canadian Club in Toronto or other service clubs across the country. But at the moment the minister refuses to answer questions put to him by members of Parliament. He keeps on putting us off by telling us that all of his answers will be in the budget, the budget which has been put back a number of times over the past few weeks. We end up with a situation where we have no answers given to us by the minister, and the only way we can find out what is on his mind, if anything, is by reading the speeches he makes outside this House.
The minister takes a great deal of consolation from the fact that 98 per cent of his Canada Works funds this year will be spent in Quebec and the maritime provinces, with a few dollars dropped off in British Columbia, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. I should like to go over the list with the minister. I should like to compare what was done last year for a whole series of communities in Canada under the Canada Works program. In Newfoundland last year the amount was $17.1 million. The minister has increased it slightly by bringing this amount up to $19.6 million. Taking 10 per cent away for inflation, we are at about the same situation as last year. Prince Edward Island last year had $3.1 million. This year it will be $3.7 million. Nova Sotia last year had $11 million and will have $11 million this year, a decrease in real terms of about 10 per cent. New Brunswick last year had $15.7 million and New Brunswick this year will have $15.1 million, another decrease of about 10 per cent in real terms.

December 6, 1979
Employment Strategy

It is very embarrassing for those good members of Parliament who were elected in the province of Ontario. It is very embarrassing to those people who went from door to door during the last campaign telling people what type of job-creation programs they would be offering.

Last year the province of Ontario received from the previous Liberal government moneys under the Canada Works program for communities across Ontario where there were high levels of unemployment and in which there were many valid social objectives to be met. They received $22 million from the Liberal government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext:
This year those same northern communities across Ontario, those same eastern and southern communities as well, which used these funds for valid local purposes and for valid social objectives, are receiving nothing. Last year $22 million

was given to municipalities and groups across the province of Ontario. The new government has taken that $22 million away from them completely and has left nothing in its place.
What have they done in Manitoba? Last year Manitoba received from the Liberal government $9.4 million under Canada Works. What is it receiving under the guidance of the new Minister of Employment and Immigration? It is receiving nothing.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: Zero.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: What is happening to the communities in northern Manitoba? What is happening to the ridings represented by members of Parliament who have undoubtedly brought their points of view to bear? I challenge the Minister of Employment and Immigration to tell me that there is no Conservative member of Parliament from Ontario or Manitoba who has not registered his strong dissent with the minister over the elimination of their provinces from the application of that program.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext:
It is the same thing in the province of Alberta which received $5 million last year and will receive nothing this year.
But let me mention also the great largesse of this government toward the people of the Yukon. This year the Yukon will be receiving something like $99,000 from this program. Last year it was ten times that amount. The Northwest Territories is receiving an amount which is almost an insult, but of course we are used to seeing insults bandied about by the present Minister of Employment and Immigration who treated in a cavalier fashion all those young Canadians presently working in one of the programs sponsored by his department. He was quoted in one of the Toronto newspapers as referring to them as "middle-class people who are looking for a job to spend a year on their own". I challenge him to come into my riding and see some of the things being done by these kids at Camp Bouchard in the city of Blainville.
To get back to the Northwest Territories, this year the government, which is interested in the north, is handing out $39,000 to the Northwest Territories under the Canada Works program. To my mind that is an insult. I am sure the people there would have preferred to receive nothing, rather than have the piddling sum of $39,000 thrown at them. Last year the amount of $2.8 million was spent by the previous government in the Northwest Territories.

In other words, Mr. Speaker, this is-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: The minister of state for unemployment development!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext:
-the present situation. Six months of inaction, six months during which the minister had time to develop policies for the new economic conditions we are going through. Rather than formulate new policies, he has been content to this day to come up with programs we introduced last year. They are excellent programs, but because they were designed last year, they are not relevant to the new economic conditions.
December 6, 1979

The minister ignored the fact that there is a recession in the United States and that under his government we are subject to the highest interest rates in our history. He totally ignored the fact that with his energy policy and his decision to increase oil prices, he is going to create, according to even his Conservative friends in Ontario and the Ontario premier himself, 137,000 more unemployed by 1981, and this is his policy, Mr. Speaker.
And now, in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to suggest to the minister two or three approaches. In my opinion, if those policies are to be consistent, they must aim at two or three objectives. There is the temporary job creation. Whether you like it or not, in our country, temporary job-creation will always be necessary to make it through the hard winter months, unless, as the minister proposes, we force people on to unemployment insurance all through the winter. We should see to it instead, Mr. Speaker, that these people are productive in our society. Now, mention is made of temporary job-creation during the difficult months, of permanent job creation, of course, and more important, manpower training, the training of skilled workers, since we know that the reservoir of skilled workers we had in the past no longer exists. We cannot depend any more on immigration to meet our needs for skilled workers. We must train those workers in our own country.
And what is most shocking is to realize, every year in September or at graduation time, that CEGEP, secondary level and university students have been trained for jobs that no longer exist. And 1 wish to ask the Minister of Employment and Immigration to set up the mechanisms required to put an end to that situation. These matters obviously come under provincial jurisdiction, but if the Minister of Employment and Immigration really wants to promote a national manpower policy, he must see to it that those young people will not undertake years and years of studies that lead to a dead end.
The minister was telling the Canadian Club in Toronto that there are going to be a number of openings for skilled workers because of the pipeline construction to come. These are new developments that are coming about. I think it is incumbent upon the minister to see to it that we cease training people in this country for jobs that do not exist and that we make a concerted effort to see to it that skilled training meets the requirements and the needs of industry.
As members of Parliament we have all had constituents come to our office and tell us about the fact that their children have gone to school for a number of years and there is nothing for them at the end of that schooling period. I tell the minister that up until now the type of system we have had in place does not sufficiently take into account the over-all employment needs of the country. I am not saying it is his fault, and I am not sure it is anyone's fault. It is one thing to have manpower needs in one province and deciding what the manpower needs are in that province, but it is quite another thing to consider
Employment Strategy
the needs right across the country. That is not the proper way to consider the problem. The proper way is to look at what the national manpower needs are right across the country. Looking at the manpower needs of one province is perhaps the way to prepare people for jobs in that province, but that closes frontiers in relation to jobs in other provinces.

Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, I would urge the minister to reconsider past decisions. The position taken by the minister today to eliminate entirely the Canada Works program, when he has absolutely no alternative to offer that idea of forcing people on unemployment is absurd. And 1 also caution the minister against the temptation to which he will undoubtedly be subjected, that is to take all existing programs within his department, to arrange them in a certain way and present them to us in a new wrapping during the Christmas season. That is not good enough.
We think there are several excellent programs within that department. We feel those programs could be rearranged, must be assessed in depth and can be somewhat reoriented. But we think the present attitude of the minister who reduces the funds earmarked for job creation and resubmits nearly everything that exists within his department in a new wrapping is not good enough. It is an approach we condemn as well as his attitude today in this area, since taking over that department on June 4 last.

I would like to suggest to hon. members opposite that there is a central fallacy in the whole philosophy of the opposition's approach to job creation.

This is a motion, Mr. Speaker, that has as its fundamental premise the notion that the government somehow must do more in the creation of jobs in Canada. I would suggest there is a fundamental fallacy in that approach of members of the opposition, because in the real world it is not the government that creates real, long-term, continuing jobs in Canada. It is the private sector which creates the real goods and services that sell in the real world.

December 6, 1979
Employment Strategy

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext:
Governments do not create the productive goods and resources in our society. Governments are merely organizing vehicles. It is the private sector, the manufacturers, the industrial strength of Ontario, Quebec, the western provinces and the Atlantic provinces, that create the real jobs which are going to last.
What government can do, what government should do, and what this government will do, is to set the right climate for the creation of jobs by the private sector. Government can supplement the job creation of the private sector, or government can provide incentives to the private sector to create jobs, but 1 emphasize and I repeat-and 1 cannot do this strongly enough-that it is not the government that creates the real, lasting jobs in our society.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext:
Let us look at the record of those persons opposite who formed the government, including the hon. member who just spoke. That government had a golden opportunity when it came into office in July 1974 with a very substantial majority-well I remember. Let us look at the record. When that government was elected there were 490,000 persons unemployed in Canada. That was in 1974. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate was 5.1 per cent. That was their beginning point and they had an opportunity then. Let us look at the record when the government was defeated in May of this year. We note that the seasonally adjusted figure indicated that 853,000 persons were unemployed and there was an unemployment rate of 7.7 per cent. That is some record-unemployment up in that five-year period, with that golden opportunity, by 2.6 per cent. The absolute number of unemployed is up by some 463,000 people. We know who these people are, Mr. Speaker. The women and the disadvantaged constitute the majority of that 463,000 increase suffered at the hands of the previous government.
There is a lesson in those numbers, Mr. Speaker. The short-term palliatives introduced by the previous government with their fancy acronyms-Canada Works, Young Canada Works, JET, JES, LIP, the Summer Job Corpse-the year-round Job Corps, together they did not succeed in reducing unemployment but rather assisted in increasing it. If a multiplicity of ill-co-ordinated, short-term, stop-gap creations was the way to cure unemployment, then the numbers should have gone down rather than up. The fundamental problems that the previous government failed to deal with have come back to haunt them in their search for band-aids.
Now hon. members opposite are saying, "Let's have more of the same. Let's have more of JET, JES, LIP, Canada Works, and all those short-term make-work projects." Those projects did not leave any lasting jobs for the young people of this country, Mr. Speaker. There is a record of continued failure, and the people of Canada let the party opposite know about it on May 22.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext:
A basic aim of this government is to stimulate long-term economic development and provide adequate incentives to the private sector which would expand and provide full-time and continuing jobs for more Canadians, and particularly young Canadians.
We have to create a climate of confidence in the country in order to achieve this, Mr. Speaker. We have to assure businessmen that the private sector can grow, that they can expand their labour force and that their community, their province, their country, is a good place in which to invest. We have to ensure that government assists the expansion in a variety of constructive ways. We have to ensure that the groups in our society which are the hardest hit by unemployment are those that benefit most by that expansion.
Direct government job creation has a role to play but it cannot be the primary means of creating jobs in Canada. It should not be the main vehicle in which a government puts its trust and its funds, because it is wasteful.
The hon. member who just spoke asks what the government has been doing for six months. That party would have people believe that the government has done very little and accomplished less. Nothing is further from the truth, Mr. Speaker. Let me put on record some facts that may be of cold comfort to hon. members opposite.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: That will not take long.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: Since this government took office, seasonally adjusted employment has risen by 232,000.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext:
What is more important, however, is that the unemployment rate, which was 7.9 per cent under the Liberal government on May 22, has fallen to 7.4 per cent, a drop of .5 per cent. The record of the last six months shows that the figure that really counts, which is the number of people not in the work force, has improved. It has not deteriorated, as was suggested.
I am an honest man, Mr. Speaker. That improvement was not merely the result of direct government job creation, nor was it a result of all the activities of this government since June 4.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: That is true.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext:
Since June 4 we have had an improved climate for business in Canada. This is shown by record levels of investment in manufacturing. We do have large portions of the country which enjoy a considerable degree of prosperity. We have record high labour earnings, and we have a developing sense of partnership in the economic progress and the future of our country.
This improved climate of confidence and of trust is not something that just happened. It was not spun out of thin air. It happened because a new government, determined to change
December 6, 1979

things, had let the people of Canada, its partners-the unions, the provinces, the private sector-know that it is looking to them to participate in economic growth. The federal government has never stated that it alone is able to solve all the job-creation problems.
In the course of the coming budget, Mr. Speaker, my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) will set out the fundamental directions which Canada must take to live and thrive in an energy-scarce world. Fie will outline the measures we must take to begin to bring our deficit down rather than up, and some of the measures we plan to take to stimulate the private sector, particularly for youth.
As early as October 16, the hon. member for Blainville-Deux-Montagnes (Mr. Fox) asked me in this House when 1 was going to bring forward my employment strategy. 1 told him then and on a number of subsequent occasions in this House, in committee and privately, that the details of the government's employment strategy would be set forth in the context of the budget, first in general terms by my colleague the Minister of Finance, and then in greater detail in the course of the budget debate. Unless the hon. member has been away or has been ill or something, he will realize that the budget has been set for next Tuesday, December 11.1 think he is aware that, in the normal course, the budget debate follows the budget. Within the next week, therefore, the full employment strategy of the government is going to be set out in this House. There has never been any doubt about that.
I would therefore ask him why a motion couched in these terms is brought before the House at this time, when he knows that if he had waited five days he would have seen the full detail of what he wants?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: It is too late.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: Hon. members opposite are very concerned about what they are going to hear next Tuesday night. They are concerned about the budget debate. They are concerned that an employment strategy will be put forward that relies on the private sector and gives it some incentive to create the long-term jobs which the previous government was unable or unwilling to create in their five years of opportunity.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member opposite knows that we have not been proceeding in a vacuum during this six-month period of planning. He knows that there is in force and operating in the field among the some 25,000 employees across Canada an employment strategy for 1979-80. That program runs, for the most part, through to the end of March, 1980. He should know that, because for a period he sat in cabinet with colleagues who created portions of that employment strategy. 1 appreciate that he was absent for a few months.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: He is still short.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext:
He realizes, of course, that there are operating programs. If we were to take his motion seriously, it would
Employment Strategy
constitute a direct and frontal attack on the programs of his own government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext:
Let me tell the hon. member some of the ongoing programs during this so-called period of "inaction" that he is referring to. I mentioned Young Canada Works. I have some reservations about that program. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, there were 6,262 projects this past summer with a total commitment of over $54 million and some 33,000 jobs. That is since this government took office.
I am sure he has heard about the Local Employment Assistance Program. It was started on a very ineffectual basis by the previous government but this government has expanded it by some $30 million to service the communities that need it most-that is, the native communities of Canada. They have responded to it in a positive way and in very large numbers. I am sure he is well aware of the grants of half a million dollars each to Guysborough county and Nanaimo under the LEDA program. These programs are creating jobs in those communities which were hard hit by unemployment.
I am sure the hon. member is also aware of the employment tax program. I am sure he knows that one because we have certainly taken some lessons from it. It created 58,000 jobs in the private sector across Canada in a year and a half, about
36,000	of them in the last year. It is a program that happens to be working. It has as its basic and principal philosophy the use of tax incentives to the private sector to create permanent jobs in our society.
I am sure the hon. member has heard of the JES program. It was operating this past summer. There were about 5,000 jobs thereby available during the summer, which is not a bad record for a new government coming into office to make a program work. Then there was the critical trade skills training program which had some difficulties. We are going to expand this program. It will give Canadians the skills they will need in the future.
Of course, the hon. member has heard of many of the other programs as well. I am not going to go through the record. There was a summer youth employment program which operated in June, July and August under the new government. Was the hon. member aware of the 293,000 cumulative placements in the public and private sector for summer jobs under that program operating under this government? The hon. member did not mention those. To have mentioned those in the context of his motion would have been to attack some of the basic programs of his government, the government which he supported, and he knew that.
1 expect to have an opportunity, I hope very shortly, to introduce legislation in this House which will help give effect to a major new youth employment program which is to begin this winter.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext:
Hear, hear!

December 6, 1979
Employment Strategy

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext:
As 1 have already indicated, it will be a program to increase the ability of the private sector to employ young people who make up nearly half of our unemployed in Canada. We will also be putting forward plans to assist the non-profit voluntary sector. In other areas this group has shown a tremendous degree of skill and tenacity as displayed in the refugee program. The same voluntary sector will have an opportunity to hire young people to carry out environmental and other important community needs projects under the national youth service corps. Finally, I will be taking measures in the very near future to strengthen our training programs to help the private sector eliminate the bottleneck in overcoming the skill shortages which, frankly, are a legacy from the previous government.
One thing I want to assure all members is that we will be achieving more jobs, and I will say it three times-jobs, jobs, jobs at less cost, cost, cost.
Our programs are not going to fritter away the funds on jobs that are here today and gone tomorrow, like the will o' the wisp in the middle of the night. We are going to replace the employment impact of the former hodge-podge of Liberal programs with a smaller number of programs, better designed to do the job. in particular they will be designed to stimulate the creation of profitable and continuing jobs in the private sector for our unemployed young people. The way in which we have gone about the reorientation of Canada Works, which the hon. member spent a portion of his time discussing today, is a good example of the sort of approach that I have in mind. I am the first to admit that in previous periods there were isolated instances where Canada Works had its successes. But it has been an unnecessarily expensive and wasteful way of trying to create artificial jobs for Canadians.
What Canadians want is not jobs that average 30 weeks, which is the experience under Canada Works. They want jobs that last, not jobs that disappear with the government funds that supported and created them in the first place or created dependency upon provincial or municipal governments. Canadians want solid, long-term job creation, not the kind that disappears and leads people right back to unemployment insurance. We will get rid of that vicious cycle of government job creation back to U1 and then back to government job creation. That is a vicious cycle, Mr. Speaker, which destroys the very creative soul of our young people in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: The opposition seems to ask why the program was not in place the day we took office. Where was your program on June 4, they ask. They know perfectly well why it was not in place.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: This is December 6, six months later.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext:
Hon. members know why it will be in place next week. Hon. members will know why it took six months to put it together. One cannot streamline and rationalize overnight a large hodge-podge of old programs, and a few sensible ones I

confess. To turn programs around and point them in the right direction takes time, thought and planning.
1 want to pay a particular tribute to officials in the Canada Employment Immigration Commission for their willingness to innovate and to respond to a philosophical direction that will put this country back in the right direction.
The program was not put together overnight, but it is put together. The important thing is that it will be done right.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: That will be a change.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext:
That is why we decided rather early on in Canada Employment and Immigration that we had no choice but to go ahead with some of the plans of the previous government, particularly to mount a further Canada Works program, on a limited basis albeit. We knew that it would not be possible to have major new youth programs operating right away, although we were comforted by the fact that there were some youth programs operating then, some effectively and some ineffectively. We decided to use the plans of the previous government as a temporary bridging device from the old to the new.
I am happy to be able to say, however, that we simply did not repeat the old Canada Works program with all its unnecessary expenditures and abuses. We deliberately chose to restrict the temporary and final phase of Canada Works to those parts of the country with the highest unemployment, the highest labour surplus rates. Hon. members opposite know that. They know the areas of greatest need. It is no secret that the constituencies of greatest need and highest unemployment are not represented by members supporting the government. Nevertheless, the money was put where the people needed it the most.
All constituencies with a labour surplus rate of over 9 per cent are receiving Canada Works funds. Any constituency with unemployment rates below that rate are receiving no funds at all. I hardly need point out that this is a very different practice from that of the previous government. In earlier phases of Canada Works large areas of the country which had relatively low unemployment rates nevertheless received funds to stimulate a temporary job creation.
Saskatchewan and Alberta had seasonally adjusted unemployment rates of 4.1 and 3.9 respectively, yet they still received substantial funding under the arrangements of the Liberal government. This was not only unnecessary, it was wasteful and in many instances it was pernicious. The city of Edmonton-I have nothing against Edmonton; I am very fond of that city-had an unemployment rate of less than 3 per cent. It received $600,000 in Canada Works funds under the Liberal government from 1978 to 1979. It is extremely difficult to understand why in an area where labour is in short supply the previous government would insist upon stimulating the demand for labour. It is pushing where one should be pulling. That is exactly what the previous government did. In many areas of the country where unemployment was either moderate or low the previous government used Canada Works
December 6, 1979

funds in a way that increased labour shortages rather than reduced unemployment.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: Table the study.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: Order, please. The Chair has been very lenient in allowing the conversations that are going back and forth between members on both sides of the House. They have not been directed to the Chair. If hon. members wish to carry on these conversations in a jestful manner, there is space provided behind the chamber. I suggest they do it out there. I ask that the remarks of the hon. minister be directed to the Chair. Let us have order in the House, please.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: Well said, sir.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will endeavour to address my remarks to you. What the previous government was doing in its Canada Works program was engaging in the kind of wasteful, unfocused and inappropriate expenditures of funds which no government, looking at the labour market demands of the 1980s, should ever tolerate. As I said, this government will not squander the funds in that manner. We have too great a responsibility to the people of Canada, who elected a responsible government-which means a fiscally responsible government-not to squander funds in that fashion.
Instead of spending Canada Works funds in the low unemployment areas of the country, we have used them to increase the funds available for the creation of medium-term and long-term employment of, for example, native people. The LEAP program, to which 1 have already made reference, has increased its budget this year by about one-quarter to a level of nearly $50 million. This money will create long-term, permanent jobs for native people in areas where they need them the most. Of course, those native people have suffered for a great many years from a lack of long-term economic development and high unemployment rates. It is a very serious situation and we will come to grips with it directly.
I think that the House and the country will agree that this money is better and more productively spent in that fashion than if it were used to increase labour shortages in Calgary, Edmonton, Regina and many other parts of the country where labour shortages actually exist. I must add that the restriction of Canada Works to the high unemployment areas of Canada and the use of Canada Works funds to assist the long-term native development under LEAP is a course of action which is heartily concurred in by all provincial governments from coast to coast.
I asked members of the provincial governments directly in July, November and December what their view of Canada Works is. Now, I can say that without exception the provincial governments have indicated to us that because of its ineffectiveness, moving toward a phasing out of Canada Works is a step in the right direction. They have, as have the members on
Employment Strategy
this side, no love of short-term, stop-gap, make-work type projects which create dependency on provincial and municipal governments and leave no long-term benefits.
It is significant that despite the suggestion of inhumane cutbacks from hon. members opposite, I have received very few complaints from the communities or individuals who are allegedly subjected to this inhumane treatment. Ordinary people know that Canada Works was not an effective program. They know that it makes little sense to create artificial jobs like these, particularly in areas where jobs often cannot even be filled. I suspect that the opposition will soon come to realize this as well.
I must make reference to the fact that the greatest number of complaints I get about the Canada Works program and its cutback are from some of the hon. members opposite who have been accustomed to the fact that they have had a so-called right of appearing to dispense local patronage in their constituencies. Somehow with the cutback, that right of dispensation of local patronage is no longer there.
Indeed, 1 am constrained to make reference to one hon. member who just yesterday was saying to me that he needed a Canada Works project in his riding to keep open the almost
1,000	miles of snowmobile trails which the tourists use to service the commercial hotels in his region. I asked the hon. member why he needed the snowmobile trails open, and he said that it was good for the business of the hotel operators. I asked him, if no Canada Works is available next year, what he intended to do. He said that the provincial government would pick it up. 1 then asked him why the keeping of the snowmobile trails open must be subsidized by the federal government. He replied that it had always been done that way. That was his answer, and he went on to say that this would be the fourth time around. Without naming the hon. member, 1 can assure him that there will not be a fourth time around on that sort of make-work project.
It is the intention of this government to build a real economic partnership with the private sector in the provinces. It is well known now that in January there will be a national economic development conference which, I hope, will be a key step in the building of that partnership. Much of the success of the measures which we will be undertaking will depend on collaboration and support from the provinces, employers and union leaders. It is fallacious to suppose that the federal government can, just by spending money in isolation, generate the economic growth and employment development which Canada must have in the 1980s. To repeat, "partnership" means a climate of mutual confidence, confidence on the part of the private sector that the goal of government is to encourage, not to interfere merely for the sake of doing so. It means confidence on the part of the government that the private sector can and will make the most of the opportunities available to provide Canadians with the goods, services and jobs that we need and can absorb.
This is not, and it must never be, a matter of mere blind ideology. Rather, it involves a certain political commitment and faith in the essential rightness of our pluralistic and

December 6, 1979
Employment Strategy
private enterprise system and a political commitment on the part of the government to encourage, rather than stifle, the creativity of private business in Canada. I fully realize that after years in which the prevailing climate was one of mutual suspicion and mistrust-certainly in the last 11 years-it may take some time for a new climate to prevail. It may take more than the six months we have had.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: Or the six months you have got.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext:
There is no doubt that this is our goal, and it is a goal that we will attain. We have already gone some distance to repair the tears in the fabric of Canadian society. I look forward next week to outlining in this chamber the youth employment program of this government. This program is just not for this winter but for the long-term future as well. We are now approaching the peak in the youth labour force, which will come around 1982, perhaps 1983. In that sense it is a shorter, medium-term problem, not a long-term problem.
Extremely high and rising youth unemployment rates have made it plain that we must take measures now to help the young people. In the mid 1980s I believe that the problem may be somewhat different. In fact, it is an economic and social imperative in Canada that if we do not get jobs for or train our young people for the skills that they will need, we will merely be creating another generation to live on unemployment insurance. This government does not intend to do that.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: Order. I regret to advise the hon. member that his time has expired. He can only continue with the unanimous consent of the House. Does the hon. member have unanimous consent?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: Provided he takes only a couple of minutes. There are too many members who want to speak today.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. I did want to mention, in my two minutes that I can utilize in this context, another serious problem, and that is the problem of unemployment among women. This government, as was indicated by the Secretary of State (Mr. MacDonald) and myself during question period today, is committed to reducing the female unemployment rate in Canada. We are committed to reducing job segregation with the ultimate aim of eliminating it altogether, and we are committed to lowering the wage gap between men and women, again with the eventual aim of getting rid of it.
I also want to mention the commitment of myself and this government to affirmative action in a promotional sense on a federal contract compliance program on a much greater and effective basis than that attempted or realized by the previous government. 1 want to reaffirm the commitment of this government to establish pilot projects in our Canada employment centres for improved service to female clients. I want to make reference to the restoration of the Liberal budget cut in the Outreach program and to giving higher priority to women as a target group for Outreach projects in various communities.
I want to talk about, develop and implement policies relating to employer exploitation of domestic workers here in

Canada on work permits. As minister responsible for immigration as well as employment, I have the power and authority to implement such programs. I want to make available for women who are training in non-traditional occupations the facilities of support services, such as daycare centres, to enable them to go into that non-traditional sort of work.
I want a model training program for women on mothers allowance in the life skill-training program for native women to be developed. This is all with a view to giving women an opportunity to enter into the work force and participate on a full basis.
If I can end on a more futuristic note, the problem of the next two or three years is youth employment. This government will meet that challenge in co-operation and in partnership with the private sector. In longer terms, perhaps, an equally if not more serious problem is women's unemployment. That is not going to disappear in two or three years, because women are in the work force, Mr. Speaker. Women are in the work force to stay. This government will create the climate, create the framework and create the programs which will allow more women to participate effectively and equally in Canada's work force. 1 look forward to developing and implementing those programs.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!
