subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). The hon. member for Lon-gueuil (Mr. Olivier) on a point of order.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. 1 apologize, Mr. Speaker, I thought you had recognized the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and as 1 had not seen him rise, I thought I had risen before him. That is all I wanted to say.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: Order, please. I recognized the hon. member for Winnipeg North.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Had the motion moved today by the hon. member for Blainville-Deux-Montagnes (Mr. Fox) been slated to come to a vote tonight, members of the New Democratic Party would have voted for the motion. But I say to the hon. member for Blainville-Deux-Montagnes that we would have done that in spite of his speech and not because of his speech.
Whenever I listen to Liberal speakers, Mr. Speaker, I am again amazed, and increasingly so, by the arrogance and gall of Liberal members of Parliament. The hon. member attacked the government-the Conservative government-for a number of reasons, and for each reason for which he attacked the Conservative government, he was attacking them, in fact, for continuing policies which were implemented and continued by
December 6, 1979

Liberal governments through all the years I have been in this Parliament.
The hon. member attacked the Conservative government because it had no employment strategy. Well, I say to him that his government, which was in office from 1963 to 1979, had no employment strategy. 1 would like to put on the record the fact that in 1970 when the present Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Trudeau) was prime minister we had in this country
420,000	unemployed and the rate of unemployment was 5.2 per cent. Eight years later, in 1978, we had nearly one million unemployed and the rate of unemployment was over 8 per cent. Mr. Speaker, that is what the Liberal government had in the way of an employment strategy.
The member attacked the Conservative government because interest rates have gone up. The record is clear. Whenever in recent years interest rates went up in the United States, the governor of the Bank of Canada recommended an increase in the bank interest rate in Canada and the Liberal government acquiesced in and approved that increase. What has the Conservative government done? It has done precisely the same thing; it has followed the advice of the governor of the Bank of Canada and increased interest rates in the same way as when the Liberals formed the government.
The member attacked the government opposite because it is permitting oil prices in Canada to move toward world prices. Well, of course, the Conservative government is pledged to increase oil prices in Canada at a faster rate than they were increasing under the Liberal government. But the objective is precisely the same. 1 see the hon. member shaking his head. This is not the time, Mr. Speaker, but we could put on record the statements made on more than one occasion by the former Liberal minister of energy, mines and resources in which he said the objective of the Liberal government was to move oil prices to where they would reach 90 per cent of the Chicago price. The hon. gentleman can shake his head, but at the right time we will set the record clear.
The member criticized the present government because there is a shortage of skilled workers. Well, Mr. Speaker, there is a shortage of skilled workers in this country. In my province of Manitoba, just last week Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting, which operates a number of mines in Manitoba, applied to the department of manpower for permission to bring in a substantial number of skilled workers from outside Canada because they could not fill their needs from within Canada. That has happened in virtually every other province in this country. Under Liberal governments we have been spending hundreds of millions of dollars each year on manpower training, yet despite the fact that we had a million unemployed we have not been able to fill the jobs in this country which call for skilled people. That is to a large extent the responsibility of the mistaken, misguided policies of the department of manpower under a Liberal government.
Let me begin by saying that unemployment is a very serious problem. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Atkey) who spoke a few minutes ago was proud of the fact that unemployment has gone down in recent months. That is
Employment Strategy
true, it has gone down in recent months, but the fact is that in October the number of unemployed went up for the first time in a number of months and there were 843,000 unemployed. In October the rate went up to 7.4 per cent. Mr. Speaker, surely the minister is aware of the fact that the United States, not only our neighbour but our biggest customer and biggest supplier, is now into a recession, one which looks as if it might be a major recession. That being the case, I think the minister and the government are making a major error in assuming that the programs which they and the former government have initiated are likely to have any serious effect on the increasing unemployment we shall see in the coming year.
Mr. Speaker, our party believes this country should aim for full employment. When we talk about full employment, we are not talking about a rate of 7 per cent or 8 per cent which some of the so-called experts-the economists in universities, in government and in private industry, all of whom have pretty good, secure jobs-are trying to explain means full employment? When we talk about employment, we are talking about full employment as described some years ago by the Economic Council, among other organizations. Full employment in Canada, Mr. Speaker, is 4 per cent, not 8 per cent or 7 per cent as some economists are now saying.
We have not been anywhere near that rate for a long time. What does that mean? The difference between full employment-that is, an unemployment rate of 4 per cent-and the 8 per cent to 8.5 per cent unemployment we have had in recent years means that in this country we have lost in each of those years in the neighbourhood of $5 billion worth of production. That means that federal, provincial and municipal governments have lost in the neighbourhood of $1.5 billion in taxation. That is the result of the failure of Liberal and Conservative governments to have as an objective and to put into effect a policy and a program of full employment.
In beginning his remarks the minister said that his government believes that the major responsibility for providing employment rests with the private sector and that it is the private sector which must provide real and permanent jobs. Nobody in this House would question that in a theoretical way. Whether the present Conservative government believes more in private enterprise than did the Liberal government is not important.
We live in a mixed economy. Large sectors of the Canadian economy were established and operated by Liberal and Conservative governments. I do not want to list them all, but I can think of the electric power systems which are publicly owned and operated in virtually all our provinces. I can think of the telephone systems in the three prairie provinces which are publicly owned and operated. I can think of Air Canada, the CNR and a host of others. That is not going to change under any government, including an NDP government, so the minister is correct when he says that the main responsibility for providing jobs rests with the private sector.

December 6, 1979
Employment Strategy
In order for the private sector to provide jobs it has to have the right climate. I suggest that it did not have the right climate under the Liberal government and that it does not have the right climate under this Conservative government. Interest rates have increased sharply in the few months during which the Conservatives have been in power. High interest rates are a disaster. For whom? For the small businessman, because large corporations do not have to depend as much on banks as do small businesses. Large corporations have internal funds. They can go to their multinational headquarters. They can go to their deferred income tax accounts, which now range in the billions of dollars.	.
In the last few months I have met many small businessmen who have told me about the high cost of keeping inventory with interest rates at 15 per cent or 16 per cent. Many of the people to whom they sell are slow in paying their bills because they have not sold their merchandise, and that is killing business.
With the exception of Italy, we have the highest rate of unemployment of any of the western industrialized countries, and the reason for that is the failure of both Liberal and Conservative governments to develop an industrial strategy. That failure has led to the deterioration of our manufacturing industries and the inability of Canadian manufacturers to compete with other corporations in Canada or on world markets. The microphones which are in front of me and every member of Parliament were built in Austria, a country which has about a quarter of the population of this country, yet it is able to produce these microphones and sell them in Canada obviously cheaper than any Canadian manufacturer can. That says something about our position with regard to manufacturing.
A large part of the reason for our difficulty is the stranglehold which multinational corporations have in many of the vital sectors of manufacturing. In the automobile industry, in chemicals, in the rubber industry-to mention just three examples-multinational corporations have virtual control. Multinationals have no responsibility to Canada as a country. They have responsibility only to their shareholders to produce the largest profits possible. I do not blame them, I blame ourselves. I blame our governments for not developing an industrial strategy to meet the needs of the Canadian people for jobs.
Given the slowdown in the economy, which is worldwide, and given the double jeopardy of the cutbacks in government activity by this government, we are going to see a sharp increase in unemployment in the next year. We are going to see that, as I said, because this Conservative government does not-nor did the Liberal government-accept the principle that it is the responsibility of governments to see that people in Canada who want to work will have the opportunity to get work.
We were critical of many of the aspects and features of the job-creation programs brought into effect when the Liberal party formed the government of this country. Some of the criticisms made by the present Minister of Employment and

Immigration and by his colleagues when they were in opposition were justified because those job-creation programs were ad hoc programs. They were put together to meet situations which the then government had not anticipated and with which it tried to deal through a whole patchwork of programs. We made these criticisms when those programs were in effect. We welcome any concrete, workable improvements, but I say to the minister that, given the fact that unemployment has increased and is going to increase even more, the cutbacks in job-creation funding implemented by his government will have a disastrous effect on the unemployed in this country.
I know that the minister has not agreed with me on earlier occasions when I said that the cutbacks amounted to about $75 million, but they are very substantial cutbacks. If they are not $75 million, they are at least $50 million. The smaller amount which is now available through Canada Works programs in those provinces in which the Canada Works program is still operating-and those are the provinces east of Ontario-and the increased LEAP funding which, when taken together with the Canada Works programs which are funded for this year and the coming year, amount to substantially less than what was available last year and the year before, is not good enough. The fact is that there is not enough money in total. The minister and his department has decided that provincial unemployment rates in Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia were lower than the 8 per cent which I think they said was the floor over which they would provide Canada Works programs. The minister should know that, even if that were true, in each of those provinces there are areas and groups of people among whom the rate of unemployment is very high. In my province, the rate of unemployment among the native people is very high, ranging from, in some reserves, 80 per cent to 90 per cent and at some times in the year to a situation in the city of Winnipeg where the unemployment rate for native people is very high while the over-all rate, as the minister knows, is relatively low. Yet the minister cut off the Canada Works funding, and I say to the minister that the LEAP funds provided for the province of Manitoba are far short of what is required to meet the needs of the native people.
My colleague from Newfoundland tells me that while the Canada Works funding has not been reduced directly in his constituency, funds which were available previously through the department of fisheries and which were used to supplement the Canada Works programs for improving harbours and wharves have been cut back this year. My colleague the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton)-and his is a constituency with a very large native population-tells me that last year $3 million was available but this year only $500,000 is available.
I say to the minister that I have tried to make it my business to be in touch with leaders of the native communities in my own province and across the country, the leaders of any native organization, whether it be the Manitoba Indian Brotherhood or the Manitoba Metis Federation-and one could go across the country listing the various organizations-and I have not
December 6, 1979

met one who has not felt and does not feel that the funding of employment programs or job-creation programs for these people is, to say the least, insufficient.
We are facing a very difficult time. Unemployment is not going to disappear, it is going to get worse. The length of time in which the people of Canada were prepared to accept the arguments of the present government that whatever their problems are is the fault of the former government has run out. The polls taken by Gallup recently which indicated that the support for the government has dropped to 28 per cent is a clear indication that the people of Canada do not accept the arguments of the present government that it is following correct policies and that it is doing all that can be done. The Liberal government which was defeated in May of this year was defeated because the people of Canada felt that the government was not dealing with their problems.
The government was elected because it promised to follow different policies. What the people of Canada are finding is that the present Conservative government is following precisely the same policies as the former Liberal government. They are indicating their disapproval. They did so in two byelections and they did so as indicated by the Gallup poll.
I urge the minister and the government to take the problem of unemployment seriously and to face up to the fact that this country and the world are facing difficult times. I urge the minister and the government to stop believing in the principle-

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I will try to be brief, and I want to thank all my friends from Quebec, the Liberals, for that dirty trick this afternoon. Only guys from Quebec could do that, and 1 apologize to the people for them. Besides, if 1 had been asked I would have gracefully given him the floor. 1 am very happy to have the opportunity to speak on this opposition motion. I also want to congratulate the hon. member for Blainville-Deux-Montagnes (Mr. Fox) for introducing the motion which reads as follows:
That this House deplores the complete inaction of the government, after six months in office, with regard to the creation of jobs, regrets the inhumane cutbacks in the Canada Works program that have eliminated hundreds of communities across Canada.
We must say to the people, Mr. Speaker, that this opposition motion is of course another opportunity for us to criticize the government and urge it to propose policies which are more

in keeping with the needs of the times. In these discussions, as in all others, we of the Social Credit Party of Canada always try to be as constructive as possible because our motto is not to criticize for the sake of criticizing. We rely on concrete proposals, faced as we are with the lack of decisiveness shown by those responsible for our financial situation and who have always been the policymakers in Canada.
When we read the motion, we realize that it insists on job creation. Here the two old parties show what they really stand for, the belief they still have in the full employment thesis, while we believe in guaranteed income for all. The Liberals, who are only slower socialist unionists than the New Democratic Party or sometimes reformed socialists, since the former prime minister was once a socialist, still hang on to the full employment theory. They have not yet been able to attune themselves to progress in all sectors.
And I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether the present government will finally revolutionize the old ideas, because Tories are said to be extremely conservative, to launch into real social reforms which will allow us to catch up on the extraordinary scientific, industrial, mechanical and even electronic evolution, so that we can achieve a humanized economic system in which each and every Canadian will benefit from our tremendous wealth.
We are living in the electronic age, I would even say the space age; yet from the social and human point of view we are 50 years behind the times. One hundred years or even fifty years ago people said right and left that one had to work to make a living; that was understandable in those days, Mr. Speaker, since the cottage industry was the basic industry and production depended on the actual number of craftsmen.
But today, now that the machine has replaced the artisan, forcing over 60 per cent of the regular labour force into unemployment, while production increased at the rate of 10, 20 and 50 times its former volume, you will agree with me that we can no longer speak the same language as our great grandfathers and even our grandfathers when we speak of full employment. And when we shout at the government, as the Liberals and the NDPs are now doing, criticizing it for not creating jobs, we are becoming increasingly ridiculous because we know, from all those years of experience we have spent here, that the jobs the government created in industry were for the most part temporary. And permanent jobs only confirm this fact. All those temporary jobs did was to modernize the industries and create new lay-offs instead of new permanent jobs. I limit myself strictly to industrial employment, deliberately overlooking employment in the service industries, because the latter always mean a new levy against the taxpayers.
We should stop talking about full employment once and for all and work hard to bring in the best possible system of
December 6, 1979

guaranteed annual income not only for all those who have been fired and replaced by machines, but also for all consumers who have no job and no income based on their production or even on their over-production or the super production capacity of our country.
What do we need to produce today? Is it machinery? Manpower? It is not machinery since it can produce three or four times more than humans. It is not the manpower either since we have over one million unemployed and even more people on social welfare. Could it be consumers, Mr. Speaker? Yet so many families cannot even afford essential food products like milk because it is too expensive. Food costs too much for them. The only thing wrong is the distribution which for most consumers is still based on the percentage of jobs. The logic of this crazy system of ours is quite simple: you don't work so you are entitled to unemployment insurance for a few weeks, but after that, nothing. Production cannot be bought without employment. The only solution that our economists could find was to force quotas on producers and fine them if they ever dared exceeding these quotas. We have that in agriculture. We witnessed and we are still witnessing the most glaring abuses of our times.
While infants and children were denied the milk they needed because their parents were too poor to buy it, farmers were forced to spill the milk of their cows down the drain. I really mean "forced", for if these producers took that milk to the dairy plant they were fined in addition to losing all their production. For instance, if they had $500 worth of milk, they were fined $500 and their production was seized and sold on the market. They were fined for their milk surplus. Such unbelievable contradictions occur because no government so far had the intelligence or the "free" will to create a system that would bring this super production to the consumer who has no access to it simply because he was replaced by a machine. For years we have been looking for means to help the worker in his daily work, and now that we have found some, the most victimized is the worker.
Today, Mr. Speaker, the official opposition is still serving us the same salad, full employment, always employment, many jobs in order to eat, in order to provide a decent living for all Canadians. It is as preposterous as ever.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot believe that there are not enough intellectuals in the opposition to suggest a distribution system which could operate concurrently with our modern production system. It is not enough to condemn the government's inaction. We have to suggest as soon as possible to this government remedial measures designed to deal with this unacceptable situation for all the Canadian people. Moreover, having been in power for six months, the government has not done much to set the economy afloat and to urge investors to create new jobs, and I repeat, urge.
I was quite pleased to hear the minister this afternoon. I personally agree with him that the government can only create
Employment Strategy
temporary jobs. I have always thought so, because necessarily permanent and well-paid jobs are always created by private enterprise. Today the Prime Minister reminds me of a captain who inherited an old damaged boat years ago and which he is stubbornly trying to lead safely into port with a big hole of $ 12 billion in its hull. I wonder whether he will reach the shore before March 31, 1980.
After all, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian public must be told that we are still living with the estimates and liabilities of the former government. There is no need to worry. The estimates for the fiscal year 1979-1980 which began on April 1, 1979 will apply until March 31 of next year. Therefore, we must manage within the current fiscal year ending on March 31. Now, the present government is trying to adapt. The first projections which the Liberals made in April 1979 were of course for the full fiscal year, and I think that the present government is trying to make the necessary adjustments due to the circumstances and current events.
That is why I mentioned a while ago the ship which is going through difficult times. It is much easier to abandon ship and tell the crew: Well, take over, it is your turn to try. Listening to the speeches a while ago, 1 felt it was exactly like that. The former government is blaming the new one for what it failed to do and should have done. But if we blame the present government, we must be fair and praise its efforts over the past six months in the area of consumer protection. To mention only the last two bills, I point out the measure extending the spouse's allowance at the pensioner's death, and Bill C-20 being considered by the Committee of the Whole, which, in addition to creating new jobs, will bring about a reform advocated by members of the Social Credit party of Canada for the past 20 years and allow the deduction of mortgage interest paid by the head of family and home owner. We have been asking for that for the past 20 years. It is not perfect. The Liberals said: You should have given everything and made it universal. Yet, this is a start. The door is now open. That is one way of reducing interest on single family dwellings, and in so doing, creating employment by encouraging young people to become home owners without having to spend 30 years working for big finance.
The Liberals will maintain that they too encouraged housing construction, and even that they helped the average Canadian to own his home, thus creating new jobs. I say to that, Mr. Speaker, that the Liberals helped first the owners of multiple unit residential buildings; and since they can avail themselves of all kinds of tax deductions on their properties, so that the money they borrowed cost them almost nothing, thanks to the deductions. As for the average owners, the former government helped them to get into debt for 25 or 30 years and at the rates of interest we know. Just think of it, the rates of interest run up to 15 per cent! Small owners were helped into debt, whi'-1' means that big finance was helped out first and foremost.

December 6, 1979
Employment Strategy
Today, those small owners find themselves on a dead end street because of the increase in interest rates. That is why Bill C-20 is so timely. And what does the government do, Mr. Speaker? Well, it tells us about finding employment for
105.000	young people from now until the end of March, 1981. It talks about the 44,000 agreements reached with employers right across Canada, which have enabled them to create over
57.000	jobs. To our mind, the Progressive Conservatives do not seem to be efficient enough. They keep talking about tomorrow, while the Liberals spoke of nothing but yesterday and while the unemployed stay with the same problem, that of being self-sufficient with regard to job shortages. Now, about the Canada Works program, this is what we read, and 1 quote:
-the cutbacks . . . that have eliminated hundreds of communities in Canada-
I was somewhat surprised to find that in the motion.
[English)

In fact, I was a little surprised to find again-1 say it again because of the shouting, but it will calm down-1 was a little surprised to find that again in the motion. When I compare with other hon. members, I think that Roberval received its fair share of the pie. Of course, I should have liked, like all my colleagues, to see a much higher total amount, although it is a million more than last year. I should have preferred to see all 156 projects submitted by the people of Roberval approved. If 1 put myself in the position of the promoters of those projects, I am convinced they all consider their projects acceptable and very urgent. The purpose of those projects is still to provide seasonal work for unemployed people who are on the labour market so they can at least accumulate additional stamps to extend their future benefits. subtopic: TABLING OF NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD REPORT

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: TABLING OF NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD REPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, under part VI of the National Energy Board Act I should like to table, in both official languages, a copy of the National Energy Board's reasons for decisions pertaining to various applications for the export of natural gas.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement to the House on the government's appraisal of our natural gas situation and on the principal elements of our policy for this important source of energy, including the question of additional exports.
First, I want to talk about the place of natural gas in our energy strategy.
Gas is a Canadian success story. We have a favourable endowment which is responding well to the development efforts of the petroleum industry. It is one of the keys to energy self-sufficiency for our country.
The extent of the resource base in southern Canada has recently been re-evaluated by provincial and national regulatory bodies. Their findings indicate that remaining-recoverable reserves of gas in western Canada are of the order of 72 trillion cubic feet, about one third more than earlier estimates.
Exploration activity in the Beaufort Sea, the Arctic Islands and off our east coast continues to turn up encouraging gas
Energy
discoveries. Of these, the finds in the Sable Island area offer some of the best opportunities for early development.
As was indicated at the first ministers' conference in November, it is the government's intention to create the conditions for natural gas to be available to more Canadians right across the country. Our priority must be to make maximum use of what we have in relative abundance. Every gallon of oil substituted by the use of natural gas contributes to our energy independence.
As the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) indicated following his discussions with Premier Lougheed last week, we are working towards an agreement with Alberta on an incentive price for natural gas. Alberta has already introduced legislation to facilitate the implementation of marketing incentives for new sales of gas.
This will enable gas distributors to expand markets by helping to support the costs of extending service and bring about conversion from other fuels. The gas transmission and distribution industry is responding with ambitious plans for the geographical expansion of markets in Quebec, the maritime provinces and British Columbia.
The substitution of gas for oil fuels in areas of Canada supplied with indigenous oil can help "stretch" our dwindling supplies of conventional crude oil while we get on with the job of developing the oil sands and heavy oils from which the bulk of our western supply may have to come in the 1990s. [Translation]
Gas has an especially important role to play in provinces which are actually or prospectively dependent on costly and insecure sources of overseas oil. The government is determined to reduce this dependence and to secure for Canadians living in these areas a stable and reliable supply of domestic petroleum energy.
The greatest opportunity is presented in the province of Quebec. There, by 1990, additional gas sales could be equivalent to 80,000 barrels daily of oil. Taken together with efforts which the province is making to develop its own hydroelectric resources, this can make an important contribution to achievement of our national self-sufficiency goal.

We will work closely with the provincial governments and the gas distributors to ensure that there is a rapid but orderly conversion to natural gas. I want to extend this undertaking especially to Ontario, whose government has requested an integrated effort to obtain maximum substitution within the physical limitations of the industry.
The federal government believes that very substantial domestic gas market expansion will be accomplished in the next decade as a result of incentive pricing and industry's planning for pipeline expansion.
There is an abundant supply for existing users. Consumers in areas already serviced can switch to gas as quickly as equipment and labour will allow. And the needs of future new

December 6, 1979
Energy
users are assured by the size of our resource base, the vigour of its development and the vigilance of our regulatory authorities.
Now, as to the matter of additional exports in the circumstances 1 have outlined, the government is fully prepared to see the export of those quantities which are surplus to our foreseeable needs for use in Canada. Such exports stimulate exploration, and success could mean more oil as well as gas, and make a valuable contribution to our trade balance.
The export of natural gas is subject to licence of the National Energy Board and approval by the governor in council. The board must be satisfied that the quantity to be exported is surplus to reasonably foreseeable requirements for use in Canada and that the export price is just and reasonable in the public interest.
The National Energy Board, which enjoys the government's complete confidence in carrying out the task entrusted to it by Parliament, has now determined that we have a significant exportable surplus of natural gas. Consequently the board is prepared to issue licences for a total of 3.75 trillion cubic feet.
The board in February, 1979, decided to apply three new tests to applications for additional gas exports. The amount of gas which the board is now prepared to license is very much within the most stringent of these, the "current deliverability test". This means that the surplus to be exported has actually been found and developed. It is not dependent on future discoveries.
The board received applications for the export of 8.8 trillion cubic feet for terms of up to 15 years. The board found it could approve the full amount of applied-for exports only through 1984, with reduced levels through 1987, and no new exports after 1987. The government agrees with the board's findings and will allow the licensing of these exports to proceed.
Hear, hear!
Shame on you!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
The government is satisfied that future Canadian requirements have been appropriately assessed and that the new exports are surplus to these requirements. These exports are short-term in nature and will be of substantial economic benefit to Canada. At today's export price, they are worth $13.2 billion dollars U.S.
I want now to touch on some of the other implications of this decision. Almost half of the new exports are for PanAlberta and will assist the pre-build of the Alaskan natural gas pipeline. In approving the Pan-Alberta exports, the board imposed the requirement that exports be delivered only through pre-built sections of the Foothills pipeline. It further conditioned approval on the understanding that the construction of pre-built facilities will proceed expeditiously for completion of the western leg by November, 1980, and the eastern leg by 1981. Should this not take place it would be the intent of the board to conduct a review of these licences.
Thus it will be up to the sponsors of the Alaska natural gas pipeline to respond with firm commitments for the entire

pipeline. The board's decision clears up any ambiguities that may have existed and thus should give impetus to the completion of the whole system.
The other half of the new exports will be shared by other exporters and these can begin almost immediately after United States approvals are obtained. The Pan-Alberta exports already have conditional approvals from U.S. authorities.
Many Canadians, I know, would be uneasy in today's oil situation about increased exports of any form of energy. However, the government is satisfied that ample provision has been made for expanded Canadian needs for gas, and that the price to be received is fair and just to us. Given the circumstances it would be hard to justify withholding these supplies from our neighbour. As the Prime Minister has said, we are not immune to economic problems faced by our trading partners as a result of oil supply problems. It is in our own interest to help reduce these.
Canada has a great opportunity to move towards energy self-sufficiency. Its achievement will in no small way depend on the wise use of our natural gas resources. This government is responding fully to this challenge.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker. I thank the minister for having sent us a copy of his statement. I regret, however, that contrary to our understanding with the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Baker) we did not get it before five o'clock and while we were assured that we would be given two hours this afternoon, it was 5.35 p.m. by the time we received the documents which were tabled.
It is better than in the past.

You will understand, Mr. Speaker, that it is difficult to read such a voluminous document in 35 minutes. This is why our comments should be interpreted in that context and we hope that we will have the opportunity to reconsider this very important matter. Just the same I would like to congratulate sincerely the minister for the quality of his French and for his effort when he made his statement. Let us deal now with the subject matter of the paper.
1 think that today we had another unbelievable statement from this government. I think this statement will be one that Canada will live to regret and that may go down in the history as one of the greatest sellouts we have seen.
To begin with, the government has its priorities all wrong. We are threatened with a shortage of oil in this country. I see members on the other side laughing at the situation. There are many people in Canada today, in eastern Canada in particular, who are not laughing at the situation, who are not joking as are these guys on the other side.
December 6, 1979

This government has its priorities all wrong. We are threatened with a shortage of oil in Canada, and in eastern Canada in particular, as has been admitted by both the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn). The government has been fiddling for the last few months with huge price increases in oil and gas in the form of direct or disguised taxes, and we are faced with the situation where eastern Canada, the Atlantic provinces, need more natural gas and need a gas pipeline to take gas to the homes and to the industries there.
What we have today is a general statement about the domestic situation, a number of platitudes that we have heard before, and then, to resolve that dramatic and tragic domestic situation, we have an announcement that we will sell 3.7 trillion cubic feet of gas to the United States. That certainly is a clear indication that this government has its priorities all wrong.
There is one good thing in this statement, and that is at the beginning where it tells us that gas is a Canadian success story and its speaks pretty eloquently about the great things that have been done in Canada. I should like to remind the minister that these things have not taken place by themselves. They have taken place through legislation that had been put forward by this government when it was in office-
Hear, hear!

-often over filibusters by the opposition.
The minister spoke about the discoveries in the Beaufort Sea, the Arctic islands and off the east coast of Canada. 1 should like to remind the minister that most of those discoveries have been done either with or by Petro-Canada over the last three and a half years-
Hear, hear!
-and that Petro-Canada today is the second largest gas producer in this country.
So is Pacific Pete.

In terms of the non-renewable resources in this country, gas is the largest non-polluting resource we have and the easiest and cheapest to transport across the country. Therefore, we should be extremely careful and cautious when we talk about exports. We should think in terms of the necessity of conserving it for future generations and of the future needs of our country. The worst thing we could do is to export gas for a fast buck or in order to support a faltering dollar, because then it will mean that down the line we will have to supply our Canadian needs with more expensive and more polluting resources, such as coal for instance. We have to be very cautious about relying upon illusory, short-term gains.
Oh, oh!

Mr. Speaker, 1 would remind hon. members that we listened with politeness and courtesy to the minister. I would hope they would extend the same courtesy to this side.
Energy
They are not taking this seriously.

And I hope they will take this question seriously, because it is very serious.
So in the short term we may increase the value of our dollar but we might very well diminish the competitiveness of our farmers, fishermen, and our manufacturing sector, by artificially propping up the dollar in the short term and finding ourselves less competitive in the world.
Therefore, if we have to have a bias, our bias as Canadians should be against any gas exports outside Canada. But let us assume that it might be possible to export surplus gas at this time. That should take place only on the basis of an overriding national interest, and only with the guarantee that Canada is getting the maximum advantage out of such a deal. In particular, no long-term commitments should be made.
In the past we know that, on the basis of information that has proven erroneous subsequently, Canada has exported gas and oil which now we wish had not been exported and had remained in Canada. It is therefore important that we approach the question of exports with utmost caution. Obviously that applies to gas in particular. It does not apply to oil since we do not have a surplus of oil, even though the Prime Minister last January made a generous offer to Japan of a non-existent oil surplus during his famous world tour.
So far as the statement of the minister is concerned, we note the vagueness of the statement about the building and completion of the pipeline which is essential. It leaves open the door to delays in the pipeline construction by extending the authorization of exports over a period of seven years and the possibility of reviewing the authorization after exports have started, therefore authorizing exports before the commitment for the building of the line has been made.
There is no word in this statement regarding swaps, and nothing about the eastern Canadian situation, the building of the Quebec and Maritime pipeline, and the possibility of exports to the northeastern states. In our view, exports of natural gas to the United States should be authorized only on the basis of, first of all, an ironclad commitment regarding the building of the whole Alaska gas pipeline. Everything has to be signed, sealed and delivered, particularly the financing plan and the financing guarantees, before we start exporting one cubic foot of gas out of this country to the United States.
Second, there must be an arrangement for swaps in this agreement with the United States so that down the line, if Canada were to need natural gas, we would be in a position to obtain natural gas from the Alaska gas pipeline which we might need in exchange for the gas we are now providing to the Americans. That would be the second point.
The third point is with regard to revenues arising out of gas exports to the United States. They should be used to ensure the initiation and completion of the Quebec and Maritime gas pipeline so that eastern Canada would be fully served in terms of gas service and so that people in the maritimes and eastern Quebec would be assured of getting natural gas at a reasonable price.
2102

December 6, 1979
Energy
Fourth, 1 find it unbelievable that the minister says it is up to the sponsors of the pipeline to come up with firm commitments for the entire pipeline, leaving out the United States government in this matter. Negotiations have taken place on this matter under the previous government with the U.S. government, and we should have a commitment from the U.S. government in this respect, as well as from private industry. Experience should have shown us that we should not be satisfied with relying only on the sponsors of the Alaska natural gas pipeline for the future building of the whole pipeline.
Why not?
The government opposite is even ready to privatize the whole of the country and to give it to the United States companies, without even dealing with the U.S. government.
Oh, oh!

The last point concerns the fact that we have a commitment for seven years on this sale. Our preference, based on discussions that have taken place with the industry and the community in general, has been for five-year agreements on exports. We are surprised that the government has been considering seven-year agreements.
Because of all these factors which are not referred to in this document and which, in our view, are fundamental to the export of such large quantities of gas, we believe that the government does not have sufficient guarantees from the United States authorities and from the U.S. purchasers of gas to protect our security in the future.
This statement is completely unacceptable to us as the opposition, as 1 am sure it is to the people of Canada. It does nothing on the building of the entire Alaska pipeline. It does nothing on the question of the Quebec and Maritime gas pipeline. It does nothing on the question of swaps. For these reasons we are very distressed and very dissatisfied with this report.
[ Translation]
In conclusion, I should like to make it clear that the opposition is deeply dissatisfied with this statement announcing the sale of a huge quantity of natural gas to the United States without getting in exchange any guarantees that Canada's natural gas supply will be secure or that eastern Canada, and more particularly eastern Quebec, will be in a position to get natural gas at a competitive price in the foreseeable future. In our opinion, once again the government has got its priorities ail wrong. While we are threatened with a gas and heating oil shortage in eastern Canada, the government announces today a big natural gas sale to the U.S. without having dealt with the crisis and without having provided any answers to the domestic problems of vital interest and concern to the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the New Democratic Party 1 want to say at the outset that we are unalterably opposed to this decision to export more natural gas to the United States. We consider this export decision shocking and irresponsible.
I find it utterly incredible that in one breath the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) is stating the real possibility of imminent fuel shortages, and in the other breath, his Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn), is approving future and greater exports of natural gas to the United States. Surely any responsible government, aware of the precarious fuel supply situation we are in this winter, would look toward the future of the energy security of Canada and keep those domestic natural gas supplies here in Canada for future use by Canadians.
In a nutshell, it appears to me that the government has put the earning of some fast bucks, and reducing our trade deficit through these exports, ahead of the long-term energy security of Canadians. I think really what has happened here is that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) is making energy policy. The Minister of Finance is concerned about the government's deficit and the state of the trade balance. He is looking toward the next election and taking the easy way out by approving these natural gas exports. We are giving away our trump card; we are selling out our birthright. It is incredibly shortsighted, given the domestic and international energy supply situation, that this government, on the eve of an energy crisis, would be approving these massive exports of natural gas to the United States.
Before I get into the critique of why I think this should not take place, 1 want to address a few comments to what 1 consider the utter duplicity and hypocrisy of the spokesman of the Liberal party. It was only last February when the National Energy Board, in a preliminary report, was talking about possible exports of two trillion cubic feet, that not one member of the Liberal party, then the government, rose in opposition to such a concept. Yet we hear tonight from the spokesman of the Liberal party that they have done a flip-flop and are opposed to this export. Indeed, the former minister of finance, in his last budget, was supportive of natural gas exports. I can only conclude that the Liberals are utterly devoid of any intellectual honesty.
Oh, oh!
Hear, hear!

On the matter of why the government is approving these exports, it said that it bases its decisions on the recommendations of that reputable agency, in the eyes of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the National Energy Board.
Every Canadian knows that the credibility of the National Energy Board is shot. Its track record at predicting supplies of energy in this country is as bad as the private oil industry itself. Only in 1971 we were told that we had over 900 years of
December 6, 1979

supply of natural gas. Then, as late as 1975, the National Energy Board predicted that we would be running short by 1985. Then, of course, when the push was on by the industry for a Mackenzie Valley pipeline, the NEB reduced its prediction and said that we would have a shortfall in 1983. Now we are told that we have a surplus and we can export.
In light of that dismal record of prediction by the NEB, surely the government should be proceeding with caution. The NEB admits that domestic gas demand will outstrip production in just 12 years. Of course this is using a new formula which reduces the estimates of reserves for our future needs.
Even the minister's own department, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, cautions against allowing exports of natural gas. They are saying that we should be more conservative in our surplus estimates; if we are to err, it should be on the side of safety.
Surely we have a brilliant opportunity here, by retaining these gas supplies, to substitute natural gas for oil in this country. 1 thought that was one of the key elements of this government's policy which would move us toward energy self-sufficiency, that is, natural gas substitution. Yet when we hear from the applicants for the pipeline to eastern Canada, the Q & M pipeline, their prediction indicates that they foresee a demand of two trillion cubic feet in excess of what the National Energy Board predicts for eastern Canada. In light of this government's commitment to substitute gas for oil, in light of the company's own projections of demands in eastern Canada, surely the government should not approve these exports. Indeed we have an opportunity as well to be developing a petro-chemical industry in eastern Canada, if we retain these reserves here for us.
I should like to quote for the minister from the 1979 policy paper which was put out by his department. It reads as follows:
The security of supply argument for retaining gas in Canada for domestic consumers provides a persuasive counter-argument to the proposals for rapid expansion of exports.
It appears to me the Tories have decided that it is more important to export gas to enable Californians to heat their swimming pools, than to enable Canadians to heat their homes in the years ahead. I consider that utterly shameful for a government which claims to represent the Canadian interest.
My leader predicted last week that the government would approve this gas export which represents a 50 per cent increase over current levels. I can only conclude that this government's energy policy is jeopardizing Canada's long-term energy security, by selling off inexpensive gas now in Alberta, in return for imposing on Canada in the future expensive Arctic and far northern gas, which will be at least four times the price of this gas that we will be exporting to the United States.
Their talk of self-sufficiency is a sham; their actions belie their promises. In this approval of natural gas exports, we see where the Tories really are in terms of an energy policy. It is nothing less than a continuation of the Liberal policy of selling out our natural resources. It is one step closer to a continental
Energy
energy policy. It is nothing short of treachery for future generations of Canadians.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to ask a question of the minister. I should like to know from him whether, in the export sale he announced tonight, he intends also to include in the bargain for export his mother and his father, his grandmother and his grandfather, his daughter and his son, his granddaughter and his grandson; all the children, sons and daughters-
Order, order!
-and all the grandsons and granddaughters of the 23 million Canadians whose heritage he is supposed to protect? Will he answer this question, please?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in response to the question, I can only say that 1 feel very sorry for the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) representing, as he does, the flip-flop position that the Liberal party has taken in respect of the matter of exports. 1 have to agree with my friend across the way, the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes), that there is no political morality in the Liberal party today and they are prepared to take any position in opposition to a progressive step. What I want to say to the hon. member is simply this. This opportunity for Canadians to expand their energy potential is a challenge which this government will accept, and a challenge which this government will carry out. 1 want to tell the hon. member that his position-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Perhaps he would like to be quiet and just listen to my answer. I listened to his question.
Then answer the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
1 say that the position is quite clear. This particular export application is one that is acceptable in relation to the foreseeable demand in Canada even with the extensive expansion that we anticipate in Canada under this particular government. The hon. member is misleading the House when he suggests anything else. He is simply not basing his case on fact. The fact is that we are looking ahead to future generations, unlike the previous government which did not plan and did not in any sort of context have an energy policy. speakeroldname: Mr. Paul McCrossan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak today on this motion because I think nothing could better illustrate the differences between the new government and the old government in our approaches to solving the unemployment problems in our country. Canada is a rich country with virtually unlimited potential, yet we have seen over the last three years one of the highest rates of unemployment in the western world.
This unemployment is particularly concentrated among our young people. At the same time as we have seen this heavy unemployment develop among our young, we have also seen industries on which our growth should be based curtailed because of a lack of skilled workers, workers which we have, too often, had to import from other countries. How could the previous government see this situation of our young people being deprived of their future develop and not attack the real problem? I do not want to suggest that the previous government was not spending money on job creation-far from it. At times they almost threw money at the problem.
However, I do want to emphasize that the vast amounts of money spent served in large measure solely to increase the deficit, rather than to develop permanent opportunities for our unemployed or to build infrastructures such as harbours on which our future wealth could be based. We all remember the previous government's attempt at addressing the serious problem of our young people through the Opportunities for Youth Program. This was a very Christian program. The government's approach was right from the Bible-if youth wanted money, the government told them, "Ask, and it shall be given you, seek and ye shall find, knock, and it shall be opened unto you." Unfortunately, the government found not that the "meek shall inherit the earth", but that the wily will find out how to get the money.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the previous government had better plans than that one. The motion today refers to "inhumane cutbacks in Canada Works programs" and refers to the suffering caused in many areas of the country through our government's actions in not extending the programs next year in all areas of the country.
Last year the total budget for Canada Works was approximately $175 million. Money was spent in all provinces regardless of how prosperous those provinces were. In addition, the budget for Young Canada Works was $62 million.
Let me deal with Young Canada Works for a moment. It would be useful to review the plan and what it was supposed to do. The objective of the program was to reduce student unemployment through useful work experience, by providing financial resources to fund projects whose objectives or method of operation contribute to the benefit of non-participants in the

December 6, 1979
Employment Strategy
following ways-stimulate job creation in the private sector, identifying permanent employment opportunities, providing services, or improving the environment.
As 1 said, every area of the country and every riding in the country received money for Young Canada Works last year. York-Scarborough was no exception. I was told last year that $50,000 would be spent in York-Scarborough on Young Canada Works. That money would be spent solely because there were enough submissions for the money. I would like to review just how the money was spent in my riding, because I think we have to look at just how inhumane the cutbacks could be, and how much suffering would be caused if the money were not spent the same way next year.
There were eight projects approved in York-Scarborough. The number one priority project was called "Save our streams". This was a group of three students who wished to encourage other groups to "adopt" a stream in York-Scarborough. Just where does "adopting" a stream fit in our long-term economic plans? Well, the stream might be sick and, if so, this project on which $5,500 was spent would prepare an extensive bibliography on streams and how to rehabilitate them. As the application notes, "Considerable time would be involved in compiling a bibliography but it would be extremely helpful to anyone interested in such topics". I do not for a moment want to suggest that the young Canadians who took part in this project ripped the people of Canada off, but I do find it incredible that under the previous government $50,000 had to be spent in York-Scarborough and that the most worth-while project the previous government could find to spend it on was "to adopt" a stream.
The second priority project approved in York-Scarborough was called "Creative Learning Experience". This program, which cost $7,000, was to provide arts and crafts, gymnastics, cookouts, carnivals, day trips and daily swim lessons to children with learning disabilities.
The third priority project, costing $8,100, related to Metis and non-status Indians in York-Scarborough. Now, my riding is the largest riding in the country in terms of population and has a large ethnic mix. We have significant Italian, Greek, Chinese, East Indian populations. In fact we probably have someone in York-Scarborough from every place in the world. However, I must admit I was surprised when I learned of the existence of a Metis and Non-Status Indian Association in my riding, and even more amazed when they applied for a grant to "research and document available information on the marketing of native handicrafts and souvenirs". Mr. Speaker, I accept this as a serious project, but I think you will agree it is a little far from the mainstream of economic life in Metropolitan Toronto.
The fourth project was called "Summer Outreach". It was designed to train library staff in story-telling for children, as well as to put on puppet shows for children.
The fifth project was called "Joie de Theatre". It received $8,400. These six students proposed to improvise a bilingual play according to the style of the Commedia del Arte, a 16th Century improvisational mode of theatre in Europe. The play
[Mr. McCrossan.)
to be created and performed would "utilize the characters, the exuberant gesture and the humour of the Commedia del Arte in a series of scenarios which deal with the French and English cultures in Canada. The scenarios will be used to acquaint French and English speakers with one another's culture. Audiences will learn colloquialisms as well." 1 think that means they will swear at each other.
The sixth project was called "Accent on First Base". As I recall from watching Abbott and Costello, "Who's on first, what's on second, and I don't know who is on third." These three students received $6,200 to hand out questionnaires to day-care centres across Metropolitan Toronto. The questionnaires were given to staff, parents and children. Parents would be asked to describe what type of activity they would like their children to participate in. Children would tell their favourite activity. After the survey, the data would be collected, analysed, and categorized within a manual.
The seventh priority project for $6,400 was entitled "Safety in Action", involving four students who would try to increase knowledge of water safety, life-saving and first-aid, through conducting assemblies and workshops in schools, camps, etc.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, my eighth priority project involving three people for $2,900 was to "Discovery Centre '79" and was to enable mentally retarded young people "to be physically active, to socialize, to learn, to explore and generally to have a good time during their summer holidays."
That was how the $50,000 was spent in my riding last year. The projects met the objectives. They reduced summer unemployment. They provided work experience. They provided financial resources, and all of the projects could contribute to the benefit of non-participants. Mr. Speaker, the motion before us today suggests that we are inhumane in cutting back on the funds for projects like these. It further suggests that we will cause suffering by not continuing these job-creation programs.
1 wish to stress that I did not edit the list. I outlined every single worth-while project that was approved in my riding. Is this the way we should be spending our money to solve Canada's unemployment problems? Is this the best use we can make of $62 million across the country? Members in the opposition are nodding their heads. They contend it is. The position of the official opposition is that in spite of the fact that the unemployment rate in York-Scarborough is 2 per cent, money must be spent on job-creation programs of this type.
The approach of the government is to get the money out into the areas of the country where jobs are scarce and where much more worth-while projects can be found. What our country needs is projects which employ people. To build for the future of Canada we feel we need to concentrate our efforts in areas of most need.
So far I have spoken about Young Canada Works. Let me now turn to our analysis of the Canada Works Program. In spite of the fact that unemployment was only 2 per cent, the minimum amount which could be allocated to York-Scarbor-
December 6, 1979

ough was $150,000 under the old rules. In July we announced that the Canada Works Program would be discontinued after the fourth and final phase, and would, in that final phase, be limited to those areas of the country with particularly severe seasonal unemployment problems. The decision to discontinue Canada Works after phase IV reflects the determination of the government to move toward an approach which will result in increased long-term employment in the private sector.
Members who have been involved with the Canada Works program over the last few years, know full well that the short-term employment created by Canada Works and other similar programs has not met longer-term needs. We need more than a band-aid approach to stimulate economic development in Canada.
Programs such as Canada Works were known to a great many people as make-work programs. They provided people with jobs for short periods of time; but they were jobs that were not meaningful. Unemployed Canadians do not want make-work programs; they want economically meaningful jobs that will allow them to make a real commitment to the Canadian economy.
One of the uses to which employment development programs should be put is to provide job experience that can be usefully transferred to other jobs. However, what happened with Canada Works in some cases is that people went from work on a Canada Works program to unemployment insurance, and then to work on another Canada Works program. We want to stop that kind of cycle and provide opportunities for people to move on to rewarding jobs in the private sector.
In some cases, Canada Works did provide communities with lasting benefits in terms of new or upgraded facilities such as tourist, harbour, or recreational facilities. However, it did not provide for projects which have contributed to longer-term economic development. Canada Works proved inadequate to combat structural, long-term unemployment. Canada Works was found particularly inadequate to support the long-term economic development our native people urgently required. It is for this reason that, when the decision to cancel Canada Works was made, it was also decided to make considerably increased moneys available to native communities through the Local Employment Assistance Program, or LEAP.
LEAP is a permanent program which provides long-term funding-for a one-year start-up phase plus three years of operation-for projects. These projects either assist in the development of an enterprise which will provide ongoing employment for project participants, or serve as a method of preparing people for regular jobs by giving them the opportunity to learn social and work skills in a supportive environment.
This fiscal year across Canada native communities are receiving $38.4 million through LEAP and Canada Works. In addition, during this year of transition from Canada Works to LEAP and in recognition of the fact that good, long-term proposals for economic development take time to prepare, the
Employment Strategy
LEAP criteria have been modified, for native communities, to allow LEAP allocations to be used during this transitional period to fund short-term activities where they relate to the long-term economic development of the native community.
Canada Works projects did result, in some cases, in permanent jobs. However, these were exceptions, for Canada Works had an extensive array of checks and regulations to ensure that people did not do anything which would earn a profit or create needs. Sometimes Canada Works projects did create needs, some of which had to be met by provincial or municipal levels of government which, quite frankly, were not too pleased to take over projects which the federal government had started and then abandoned. However, in other cases the requirements not to create needs meant that long-term, economically viable jobs which provided real goods and services were rare.
This government is committed to the creation of enough jobs to ensure a satisfactory level of economic growth to allow Canadians to make their own distinctive contributions to society. We know that if we want real jobs that will provide us with economic growth potential, we must look to the private sector.
Our task as a government is to bring forth initiatives which will encourage the creation of those jobs and encourage the private sector to play its full role in developing new employment opportunities. To that end we will, in next week's budget, be proposing incentives for private employers to provide up to
105.000	jobs for young people. In addition, we will provide youth with training they need to meet the needs of Canadian industry and establish a national youth service corps.
The national youth service corps will differ from the employment development initiatives of the past in that it will be targeted to those young people who most require help in finding work.
This government is committed to directing the money available for employment development to those areas where it is most needed and where it will do the most good. As hon. members know, we are examining the concept of universality in our social programs, and the same idea extends to our employment development programs. Youth unemployment is a problem of vast proportions in Canada, but certainly not every person between the ages of 15 and 24 needs our help. We will limit programs like the national youth service corps to those young people who can most benefit from them.
During the first three phases, Canada Works created
107.000	short-term jobs at a cost of approximately $510 million. We think we can use the money available for employment development to create real jobs in the private sector which will last and lead to the creation of still more jobs. In that way we hope to invest our money more wisely than has been done in the past.
Finally, 1 would like to underline the fact that my own riding did not receive an allocation for the final phase of Canada Works as a result of our government's decision, and 1 can see the reason why.
We need more than a band-aid approach to stimulate economic activity. We need more than simply throwing money

at problems. We need to compare the alternatives and choose the best ones to use our scarce resources. We need to ask piercing questions. These were all in place, and they created thousands of jobs for our young Canadians across Canada.
The minister cannot have it both ways. In one voice he is criticizing what the past government has done, and in the other he says, "Now we are going to expand it." Boy, that is some great idea! He takes the ideas which are in place, he criticizes them, and now he says they are so good that he will continue with them and expand them. And now, Mr. Speaker, I must say that only six provinces and two territories got some of the money that was allocated for the entire country. Ontario has received nothing, and neither did Manitoba, Saskatchewan nor Alberta, Mr. Speaker. And to think that six or seven months ago, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Alexander) said in this House that we, in the Niagara peninsula, had a 14.6 per cent unemployment rate. [English]

It was to train young people to be able to get into the work force, to get experience, and to take their places as productive members of our society. We had a program in place for job experience training. We paid up to $2 per hour in subsidies to the industries that wanted to take in these young people, teach them, and show them a trade. Now what do we get? We get this "great" sum by this government that was all involved and worried about the people of Canada. What will they give people in small business? It will be $1.25 an hour!
What we had was something that was working and was workable. For example, in the large urban areas of Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver, we had subsidies of $1.50 an hour to
the employer up to 26 weeks. In the areas outside of these centres, it was $1.75. In areas such as the Gaspe and the Atlantic region, there was up to a $2 subsidy, because these were areas where indeed money must be put to get people working again. At least that would give them the dignity of work; they would know their worth and feel it as Canadians who are contributing to our society.
