subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to participate in this debate this evening on the motion of the hon. member for Blainville-Deux-Montagnes (Mr. Fox) which deplores the inaction of the government on employment strategies and efforts to create jobs. In part it reads as follows;
-regrets the inhumane cutbacks in the Canada Works program that have eliminated hundreds of communities across Canada-
1 question whether the hon. member is really serious in presenting this motion. It appears to me, if we are to take his motion seriously, that it constitutes an attack on the programs of his own party. The make-work or job-creation programs in place right now were the brain children of many programs brought forward by the Liberal government when it was in power. If he has any complaints about the fundamental basis of those particular job-creation programs, he has to look to the philosophical basis of those programs instituted by his own party.
For years we looked to the Liberal party for an employment strategy to take care of the serious unemployment problems in many areas of the country. We looked for programs which would create long-term jobs, long-term employment, and jobs which would not be dead end ones paying starvation wages. But we really did not find them, certainly not from the point of view of my part of the country. In my riding all the jobs which were created were dead end ones, because no matter what

December 6, 1979

experience individuals obtained working on these particular jobs, there was no other employment to go to afterwards.
There was a continuing cycle of dependency on Canada Works programs in one part of the year, and unemployment insurance in another part of the year. My constituents are quite perceptive in this because they saw that all Canada Works programs did for them was provide a little bit of income to tide them over to the time when they could collect unemployment insurance afterwards. Nobody recognized these dead end jobs as anything other than a glorified form of welfare.
I have a little quote which demonstrates the cynicism of some people in Newfoundland about particular make-work or job-creation programs. It was quoted in the report of the People's Commission on Unemployment which was released last year. They quote from a submission from a town called Roddickton, which is not in my riding, as follows:
Job creation is like ice cream work-melts away when the good weather comes.
That has been the order of the day for the last dozen or so years. All we had from the Liberal government was ice cream work, work that melts away when the good weather comes. Between 1971 and 1978 almost $114 million was spent in the province of Newfoundland on make-work or job-creation programs. It created almost 50,000 part-time or short-term jobs, for a total of 4,100 projects. That was fine for the time, but when those projects were finished it left the province of Newfoundland in precisely the same position as it was before. To give a little bit of credit, that is not quite true as there were some good projects.
In fact I found it quite interesting to listen to the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McCrossan) on the one hand talk about how terrible and wasteful the projects were, and the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Parent) on the other hand talking about how wonderful the projects were. 1 suspect the truth is somewhere in between. Some of the projects were excellent.
In my own riding many communities got harbour facilities, wharves, breakwaters, and community halls through the Canada Works program. Many other programs were just total waste, and everyone in every community in my riding has a story about the type of waste that occurred.
This motion today demonstrates a tremendous cynicism on the part of the Liberals who present this criticism of a program that they themselves instituted. It is a program that provides really nothing for the unemployed people in high unemployment regions of the country.
To his credit, and this is about the only bouquet 1 will give the minister this evening, the minister has seen the deficiencies of Canada Works and has said he is going to replace it in the coming fiscal year. He has seen the need for a replacement for Canada Works, and 1 will deal with this from the perspective of my own riding, as a basic need for decent jobs of a permanent nature. One of the difficulties in respect of Canada
Employment Strategy
Works jobs is the starvation wages they offer, and these wage levels are not uniform across the country. Because the wages were tied to minimum wages in each province, the wages paid in my province of Newfoundland were the lowest in the country, and starvation wages at that. In real terms the wages paid under the old LIP program were higher.
There was a tremendous amount of waste in many of the projects that were presented. Many were work projects that did nothing more than make work, and there were no new additions in communities. They were simply an excuse to bring more money into the community for very temporary periods of time.
The serious problem with the whole concept of make-work programs is that they create a dependency cycle among individuals and communities for this type of annually injected but needed money. As a result, it becomes almost impossible for people in communities to survive in any other way as there are not other jobs in particular areas and they are forced to accept the type of dead-end, short-term jobs that these programs provide.
However, in the absence of any alternative it is irresponsible and cruel to take from many ridings and many areas of this country the only employment opportunities for many individuals. It has been said by the minister that it is more efficient to concentrate these efforts in areas of high unemployment. That makes sense, but what it does not recognize is that there are pockets of high unemployment in areas of this country that still need some sort of additional government input to tide the people over difficult times.
The cutbacks the minister instituted this year in the absence of an alternative program for particular areas with high unemployment rates, became a very cruel and irresponsible move on his part. The whole cutback program of the government in the last few months really belies its commitment to an employment strategy. The cutbacks in my province from the federal government perspective and from the perspective of the provincial government, both Tory governments, compounded the problems of administering Canada Works programs. Many of the projects, again referring to my own riding, only had funds provided by Canada Works for part of the job or the needed facility, such as a harbour facility.
The cutbacks in the small craft harbour budget under the Department of Fisheries and Oceans has meant that many projects are left high and dry, with no possibility of getting off the ground this year or in any other year. This points to another serious difficulty in the whole Canada Works program.
Over the last few years provincial and federal departments have seen in the Canada Works program an excuse to cop out of their own responsibility to provide wharf facilities and harbour facilities and other things under the federal Department of Fisheries. They have said, "let Canada Works do it," and that has led to very tragic and very expensive results. Some of these projects could not be done adequately under the constraints of the Canada Works program.

December 6, 1979
Employment Strategy
There was one case, again in my own riding, of a project that was instituted before 1 became the member for the riding. A breakwater and wharf were under construction with the use of labour-intensive methods under Canada Works, when what was really required was heavy equipment and machinery to do the thing properly. Since it could not be done properly with human labour, the job was not sturdy enough to withstand the ice in the winter, and when the ice left in the spring there was nothing left of the harbour facility. What this did was force these particular communities into using a vehicle for the creation of certain facilities that was totally inappropriate to the facilities themselves.
1 referred earlier to the decision of the department to cut out areas with low unemployment rates, and I said that was a good idea in theory. Let me refer in particular to the riding of a colleague of mine, the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy). His riding in Manitoba has an unemployment rate of something in the order of 75 per cent because the riding has a large native population which is excluded from the true unemployment figures. We have seen this concept of hidden unemployment all across the country. What happens is that people know there are no jobs so they stop reporting to the manpower offices.
Statistics Canada figures do not include chronic unemployment areas and, worse still, a riding such as Churchill is in a double bind because not only have they been cut off from works programs, they have also been cut off or have had programs through Indian Affairs frozen, for example, the Indian Economic Development Fund, and only emergency funding is now avaiblable. The cutback program of the government has given that particular riding a double whammy.
Let me now refer to the minister's commitment in relation to a real employment strategy in Canada to help the unemployed people who live in various regions of the country. He has made a commitment to do this through the private sector. Many times hon. members on the other side of the House have criticized us for what is termed our blind adherence to ideology. They have an ideology as well, privatization, and that blinds them to the realities in certain areas of the country where the private sector and the market economy have totally failed to alleviate real chronic unemployment problems.
To cut off make-work programs and turn the solutions to the unemployment problem over to the private sector, in my part of the country is to turn it over to a non-existent entity. Those on that side want privatization. I say that is blind adherence to a mindless ideology that just does not make sense when viewed in the context of particular areas of the country. The entire Atlantic region has been held by this government, as it was by former governments, through their adherence to an ideology which maintains a high rate of unemployment in the area without offering any means to improve conditions.
I should like to refer to the minister's final remarks this afternoon when he announced the government's commitment to alleviating unemployment among women. He said that

programs will be announced within the next few months which will alleviate the problem. I should like to examine the record of the last six months so that we may know what to expect in the future.
The Liberal government cut $3 million from the Outreach program when they left office; then the Tories promised to reinstate the funds. According to the minister, $1.3 million will be reinstated in this fiscal year and $1.7 million in the next fiscal year. This year $300,000 to $400,000 of the $1.3 million will be allocated to women's Outreach programs. Although this statement was made last September, none of the funding has been disbursed to this point.
The government's only real response to the unemployed people of this country was to cut back on unemployment insurance benefits. That was their only-they would say positive but I would say negative-response to unemployment problems. Last year the Liberals raised the eligibility requirements for part-time workers and seasonal workers. The majority of these are women. The specific regulations that would have brought those changes into effect were not enacted by the Liberal government, but were by the Tories when they came into power. At the time the minister said he was committed to putting into effect what the Liberals had done, but I would remind him that as minister he has the power to make changes and he could have changed it in June or July.
The government's commitment to affirmative action has been sadly lacking. This program, instituted by the former government, and in place for two and one-half years, is based on the voluntary agreement of the private sector to institute such programs. But these programs lack teeth, Mr. Speaker. Figures issued this week show that the income gap between men and women has increased, yet just today the Secretary of State (Mr. MacDonald) announced that he was not prepared to put teeth into the affirmative action program but would continue to evaluate the work of the voluntary sector.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext: Give it a chance.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT AND JOB-CREATION POLICY
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, it has not worked in three years. In that time the gap has widened and the position of women, relative to the over-all labour force, has become worse. Yet there is no commitment from the government that it will improve the situation.
The most telling thing is what the government has done in its own shop. The public service has become the target of cutbacks, and 60,000 jobs will be cut, 35,000 of them in the "controlled" public service. A disproportionate number of these jobs will involve women, since a major method of cutting back will be by attrition. Women in the public service are historically more mobile and leave their jobs more frequently than men. As a result, the proportion of women in the public service will drop, but the government refuses to commit itself to reversing that trend.
Buried in the government's campaign promises last spring was a pledge to provide day care in government buildings, but no initiative has been taken on this. I think most hon. members would agree that if women are to achieve equal status in the
December 6, 1979

public service, or in any other sector, day care is a necessary adjunct to the working environment.
The motion before us today deals with the need for an employment strategy, job-creation programs, and the failure of the government to do anything about these things. I maintain that both the former Liberal government and now the Conservative government have totally failed the people of Canada. All that has been provided are dead-end jobs in these make-work programs-jobs that lead nowhere and jobs that have elicited cynicism on the part of the unemployed, and which do nothing to solve the underlying cause of unemployment.
On page 87 of the report of the People's Commission on Unemployment there appears the following statement:
Job-creation programs can be seen as attempts by the government to keep people committed to the economic and political system, when in fact the high levels of unemployment are telling people that the system does not work, at least as far as their own interests are concerned.
I should say this report was prepared after hearing from hundreds of unemployed people in Newfoundland. That quotation tells us that the people of Newfoundland in particular, and I suspect people all across the country, recognize that the job-creation program is a sham. It is an effort on the part of each government to cop out of its serious responsibilities without making a serious attempt to alleviate the unemployment problems in many parts of the country.
The hon. member for Welland referred to the some 280,000 jobs that were created by the Liberal government from February, 1977, to 1978, but he did not tell us that most of them were dead-end jobs which came about through these job-creation programs. Governments have used these programs as an excuse for not providing proper economic development.
1 see my time is just about up, Mr. Speaker. I wish to thank the House for its indulgence.

In view of the present rate of unemployment, which is especially high in Quebec and in the maritimes, job-creation
Employment Strategy
programs such as the Canada Works program serve a particular purpose, that of giving workers who are temporarily out of work or in between jobs the opportunity of using their expertise for the benefit of the community on projects subsidized by the federal government. It is important to note, however, that this job-creation program, whose role remains very important in Quebec and in the Atlantic provinces, cannot be considered an effective tool against structural unemployment. A program such as the Canada Works program can only lower cyclical or ' seasonal unemployment. This program is for workers who are temporarily out of work or for those who want to get some experience in a particular field over a few months, which can help them land a permanent job afterwards.
A program such as the Canada Works program also helps community groups undertake certain projects which, without government assistance, would never get started. In a number of communities throughout Quebec, for instance, Canada Works projects have helped improve the welfare of some members of the community or the community as a whole. For instance, in my riding of Lotbiniere, this year, the Canada Works program provided work to about 80 persons who will now be able to help their community. Of course, last year the subsidy was much higher in my riding but at that time the rate of unemployment was also much higher than it is now.
Permanent jobs were created which gave people a chance to find employment; this will eventually be much more profitable than the temporary jobs created by Canada Works programs. That is the type of program the government is putting forward. In addition, the diversity of those projects calls for a wide array of skills. Sometimes those temporary jobs may also lead to permanent employment.
As we all surely know, the Canada Works program subsidizes projects in areas where the unemployment rate is particularly high, where the need for help is the greatest. That is why there are no projects this year in some cities such as Calgary or Edmonton, while there are in Rimouski, Gaspe and Bathurst. Mr. Speaker, it is this ability to relieve unemployment in those areas which have special need for assistance that makes the Canada Works program worth while.
The projects we subsidize in Rimouski, in the province of Quebec, meet the specific needs of that city in terms of employment. We do not subsidize projects that use workers in areas where there are job opportunities. So, by granting Rimouski, for instance, $73,000 for a cultural centre, we are sure that the project will hire local workers who will be employed until such time as a permanent job becomes available. We keep encouraging workers to look for a permanent job while working on a Canada Works project.
Faced with a particularly high rate of unemployment among the young workers of Canada, and especially those of Quebec and the maritime provinces, the Canada Works program very often reaches a double objective, preventing their going through a long period of unemployment and sometimes provid-

Mr. Speaker, I prefer by far seeing our young graduates from the various community colleges work on the construction of a system of cross country ski trails while waiting for permanent jobs than wasting their time standing on street corners.

According to demographers, the post-war demographic explosion ended around 1960. And while in the first half of the 1980s we will have to deal with young people wanting to find a place for themselves on the labour market, the situation will reverse itself afterwards. The further we will go into the decade, the more the age pyramid will change: young workers will no longer be the majority but rather middle-age workers.

Peninsula, the middle age population is in dire need of this vocational training. Let us not wait the mid 1980s to meet the needs of these workers. They are the ones who, in our area, did not have the chance to make advanced studies and to attain a high level of education in order to compete in labour markets where manpower is more restrictive. They have to be content with being part of a second-grade labour force which always gets the jobs that provide hardly any employment security. Further, they have to accept lower salaries and fringe benefits. Finally, they have almost no promotion opportunities. That is why, Mr. Speaker, occupational training is extremely important to people in that social stratum.

The government will also put the accent on its work-training programs, both in industry and in technical schools.
